A Multiverse of Magic.name: A Multiverse of Magic
A Multiverse of Magic.text:
Heroes delve into ancient ruins, discovering magical treasures in forgotten halls. Champions face an enraged dragon, their blades pulsing with magic, and are bathed in its devastating breath. Adventurers search a legendary wizard’s tower for spellbooks and discover—to their horror!—the wizard has become a terrifying lich.

Magic is a defining element of Dungeons & Dragons games. Arcana Unleashed is a celebration of the magic we love as D&D players; it’s full of new and updated magical character options as well as advice for crafting your own magical worlds for your players to explore for years to come.

Alustriel’s Arcana.name: Alustriel’s Arcana
Alustriel’s Arcana.text:
In this book, the archmage Alustriel Silverhand from the Forgotten Realms setting—a human daughter of the god of magic Mystra and paragon of righteousness and virtue—presents arcana she has discovered during her travels. (You can learn more about Alustriel in Vecna: Eve of Ruin.)

But the contents of this book can be used in any setting, whether it’s the Forgotten Realms, Ravenloft, or one of your own making. Think of this book as a toy box full of options to incorporate into your game as the Dungeon Master chooses.

This book relies on the rules in the Player’s Handbook, Dungeon Master’s Guide, and Monster Manual.

Using This Book.name: Using This Book
Using This Book.text:
Chapters 1 and 2 include character creation and play options and are suitable for all players; the remainder of this book is intended for DMs only. The chapters cover the following topics:

Chapter 1: Character Options. This chapter presents eight subclasses, ten backgrounds, and more than two dozen feats perfect for creating characters who inhabit a magical world.

Chapter 2: Spells. Dozens of spells offer new options for spellcasting heroes.

Chapter 3: Creating Magical Worlds. This chapter presents guidelines for making magic a central part of your game, with examples from D&D settings, and examples of magical group patrons to inspire your games in any high-magic realm.

Chapter 4: Magical Factions. Nine organizations of magic aficionados—one affiliated with each school of magic, plus one magical saboteur group—provide powerful allies or fearsome foes.

Chapter 5: Magic Items. This chapter presents myriad new magic items to fill your magical hoards, plus rules for magic items that grow in power alongside the player characters.

Chapter 6: Magical Creatures. This bestiary includes statistics for eight specialized archmages, minions warped by foul magic, living spells, the fiendish villain known as Venger, and more.

Appendix: Tomb of the Shadow Serpents. This adventure for level 1 characters presents a challenge from Venger to claim treasure or die trying.

Erion Makuo

The Weave of Magic

The worlds within the D&D multiverse are magical places. All existence is suffused with magical power, and potential energy lies untapped in every rock, stream, and living creature—even in the air itself. Raw magic is present in every manifestation of energy throughout the multiverse.

Mortals can’t directly shape this raw magic. Instead, they use a fabric of magic—an interface between the will of a spellcaster and raw magic. The spellcasters of the Forgotten Realms call it the Weave and recognize its essence as the god Mystra, but casters have varied ways of naming and conceptualizing this interface.

Whenever a magic effect is created, the threads of the Weave intertwine, twist, and fold to make the effect possible. A spellcaster surrounded by the Weave can shape lightning to blast foes, transport hundreds of miles in the blink of an eye, or even reverse death.

But in places where the Weave is damaged, magic works in unpredictable ways—and if it’s torn, raw magic is inaccessible. Even the most powerful archmage can’t light a candle via magic in an area where the Weave has been torn.

My Esteemed Heroes,

Magic thrums through our multiverse. Powerful magic can save or destroy worlds, though magic’s balance is as delicate as a thread.

For centuries, as a daughter of the goddess of magic Mystra, I have protected the Weave and fostered the good in all creatures, lest wickedness snap the Weave.

This has happened more than once, and the resulting suffering was immense. To prevent the unthinkable, magic must cultivate love, joy, and hope and banish hatred and pain. While I draw breath, I shall pursue this cause.

My friends—heroes—I hope you will join me.

However, I know you can’t join my cause without knowledge of magic’s greatest wonders. And so I bequeath in this tome arcana I have collected throughout my long life.

I hope you use this arcana to better your worlds, but I can’t make that choice for you. I simply reveal the gifts of my divine mother and trust you will use them to do good.

May Mystra smile on you always,

Schools of Magic.name: Schools of Magic
Schools of Magic.text:
The eight schools of magic that underlie spellcraft are key to this book’s magical character options, and its magical factions and tools for building magical worlds are tied to the schools’ nuanced characteristics. The following entries expand on the schools’ brief descriptions in the Player’s Handbook:

Abjuration spells include protective and healing magic, as well as magic that prevents or reverses unwanted effects.

Conjuration spells involve creating objects and effects, summoning creatures, or teleporting.

Divination spells allow the caster to peer into the future or other planes of existence to gain helpful or bolstering benefits or information.

Enchantment spells include magic that bends targets’ minds to the caster’s will.

Evocation spells create physical effects that are often spectacular and might include destructive energy such as fire, cold, and acid.

Illusion spells include magic that creates sounds, images, smells, and other sensory effects that deceive the mind or senses.

Necromancy spells manipulate life and death, including restoring the dead to life, animating undead creatures, and siphoning life from the living.

Transmutation spells include magic that transforms creatures and objects, granting characteristics and abilities they previously lacked.

Baelnorn.name: Baelnorn
Baelnorn.text:
Undead Protector of Ancient Sites

Habitat: Forest, Urban; Treasure: Arcana

Baelnorns are deathless guardians of treasures and lore. Each baelnorn was once a living person who undertook a non-evil process to preserve their existence that involved either a divine blessing or an ancient ritual. Many baelnorns were once elves. In fact, ancient elves were the first to discover the secret to becoming a baelnorn.

Baelnorns typically dedicate themselves to protecting vaults, castles, or ruins. In the Forgotten Realms, elf baelnorns protect the site of Myth Drannor, a ruined ancient city that was once a magical metropolis. Many enjoy studying ancient lore lost to living scholars. As only the most dedicated can endure the transition into a baelnorn, baelnorns are often proud of the eternal life they’ve achieved.

Unlike liches, baelnorns almost never have soul jars, although some baelnorns associated with a holy site might house their souls within a sacred relic. Many baelnorns create magical clones their spirits can inhabit if their bodies are destroyed.

Newly risen baelnorns look much as they did in life, albeit with glowing white eyes. They often continue their prior roles as guardians, sages, or teachers. A baelnorn’s hair and flesh gradually fade away over many years; the oldest resemble stately skeletons in diaphanous raiment.

Baelnorns spend years poring over arcane tomes to aid their transition into undeath, and even those who weren’t mages at the time of their transformation typically spend much of their long existences studying magical lore. As a result, baelnorns can cast powerful spells.

Baelnorn Lairs

Most baelnorns guard sites of historical or spiritual importance, sometimes long past the time anyone living remembers the sites. A few baelnorns instead guard great secrets, artifacts, or significant family lines, usually within such ancient sites. A baelnorn’s protected site might be a grove of supernatural trees, the ruined capitol of a long-lost nation, or a library holding eons-old magical lore.

A baelnorn extends its presence into the region it inhabits, creating the following effects:

Projection. While in its lair, the baelnorn can cast Project Image, requiring no spell components and using Intelligence as the spellcasting ability (spell save DC 19). The spell’s range is limited to the baelnorn’s lair.

Travel Ward. Creatures can’t use teleportation or planar travel to enter or exit the lair.

If the baelnorn is destroyed or moves its lair elsewhere, these effects end immediately.

Most baelnorns embody the ideal of scholarly focus and self-sacrifice for the benefit of society. If you meet one, I suspect they’d appreciate sharing a lively conversation or ten. Forever can be a lonely existence.

Goals and Activities.name: Goals and Activities
Goals and Activities.text:
The Bejeweled Conclave seeks to increase its sway across the multiverse. The faction engages skilled diplomats, courtiers, and entertainers and hones their abilities. Enchanters and spies receive a more clandestine, but no less thorough, education. The conclave prizes subtlety and secrecy above all; members are taught that it’s better to fail a mission and keep the conclave’s secrets than to succeed at the cost of exposing the faction’s true goals.

The Bejeweled Conclave operates in major cities throughout the multiverse. Distance keeps members from knowing all their peers, but the faction is quick to celebrate successes, building loyalty and camaraderie within its ranks. While all members learn conversational tricks to offer convincing praise, the compliments members bestow on each other are usually genuine.

Conclave members understand that overtly using Enchantment magic risks exposing them as more than entertainers and courtiers. If a member must modify a noble’s memories or magically dominate a general, they undertake significant planning to conceal their involvement.

Leadership and Organization.name: Leadership and Organization
Leadership and Organization.text:
@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.book.JournalEntry.aunArtHandoutsG2.JournalEntryPage.4ME0lPAo3cxfB6xU classes=overlay-caption cite=false]

More experienced members of the Bejeweled Conclave oversee operations assigned to junior members. Valuable secrets are reported through this hierarchy up to the faction’s highest ranks, referred to as the Whisper Network. These leaders hoard a treasure trove of secrets; there are few facts about the movers and shakers of civilization that the Bejeweled Conclave doesn’t know.

Conclave members are trusted to act alone when necessary, such as when an important client insists on hiring only a single mediator or companion. When possible, though, senior members politely request that their “junior clerks” or “associates in training” handle more workaday aspects of their affairs. Such requests, which might include subtle magical compulsion, are a ruse to bring another trained member to operate from the shadows. As a result, clients who planned to planned to hire only one member of the Bejeweled Conclave often find themselves engaging two or three.

Whisper Network

Members of the Whisper Network keep their identities private, even from their peers. The only exception is Madame Hestia Ilverne (Medium @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmNobleProdigy00]{Noble Prodigy}), a courteous human Whisper Network member who heads the conclave’s public-facing efforts. Rumors within the faction claim that Madame Ilverne is among the lowest ranked of the leaders, but she seems nothing but pleased with her position.

Whether members of the Whisper Network work as music instructors, clerks, dancers, or cooks, they keep an eye on all aspects of Bejeweled Conclave activities. If they have edicts or missions to impart, they do so through Madame Ilverne. When she casually mentions a task to a member with the words “The Network would prefer a favor,” all comprehend the seriousness of the request.

Lurewood Mansion

A regal manor house in the garden district of a major city, Lurewood Mansion is the conclave’s academy. The previous owners donated their property generations ago for unknown reasons. The manor’s architecture has been adapted to include numerous salons and studies, as well as a fine kitchen.

In the studies, members of the Bejeweled Conclave learn to negotiate deals and defuse arguments. In the salons, singers, dancers, and musicians practice entertainment suitable for elevated private parties, from subdued chamber music to sensual dances to heart-wrenching ballads. New faction members take lessons here no matter how polished they are when recruited, if for no other reason than to bolster the illusion that negotiation and entertainment are the Bejeweled Conclave’s prime objectives.

Beneath the mansion, a dizzying maze of chambers connected through locked doors and one-way mirrors facilitates practice in eavesdropping, lock-picking, quick changes, and stealthy escapes. Other rooms allow members to rest out of sight. The heart of the maze contains the mansion’s best-kept secret: workrooms where enchanters teach apprentice mages the arts of twisting minds, magically hiding secrets, and erasing memories.

Joining the Conclave

Aspiring faction members can’t join the Bejeweled Conclave by requesting admission; members inevitably deny that there are any openings in what they claim is simply a loose professional organization.

Entry is only by invitation. Senior members carefully watch entertainers and mediators who have impressive public reputations. Those who seem particularly shrewd and ambitious might receive an invitation for free training in their specialties at Lurewood Mansion, hosted by Madame Ilverne.

Once an invitee arrives, Madame Ilverne engages them in cryptic conversation. If the potential member impresses her with their poise, acumen, and discretion, she invites them to join the faction. Otherwise, she thanks them for their time and sends them on their way without ever indicating that the mansion is anything other than a professional academy.

Renown Rewards.name: Renown Rewards
Renown Rewards.text:
Characters gain renown with the Bejeweled Conclave by sharing valuable secrets or completing conclave missions. As their Renown Scores increase, they gain access to various perks, as shown on the Bejeweled Conclave Renown table. If your campaign doesn’t use renown, the DM decides if and when characters earn these perks.

Bejeweled Conclave Characters.name: Bejeweled Conclave Characters
Bejeweled Conclave Characters.text:
Joining the Bejeweled Conclave is advantageous for any character with mysterious allure, regardless of whether they use magic to enchant others. Those skilled at uncovering and trading secrets are also well suited to this faction, as are entertainers who specialize in dancing, singing, or other performance arts.

The most sought-after recruits are @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.classes.Item.phbbrdBard000000]{Bards}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.classes.Item.phbrgeRogue00000]{Rogues}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.classes.Item.phbscrSorcerer00]{Sorcerers}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.classes.Item.phbwlkWarlock000]{Warlocks}, or @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.classes.Item.phbwzdWizard0000]{Wizards} (especially those with the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.subclasses.Item.aunEnchanter0000]{Enchanter} subclass; see chapter 1). Characters with proficiency in Deception, Performance, Persuasion, or Sleight of Hand or who have the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.backgrounds.Item.aunBejeweledCoUU]{Bejeweled Conclave Spy} (see chapter 1), @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.origins.Item.phbbgEntertainer]{Entertainer}, or @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.origins.Item.phbbgNoble000000]{Noble} background are also likely to be recruited.

Member Benefits

If you’re a member of the Bejeweled Conclave, you receive these benefits.

Finer Things. The conclave ensures its members dress well, paying you a stipend that supports your Wealthy lifestyle (4 GP per day).

Trinket. Roll on the Bejeweled Conclave Trinkets table to determine what trinket you have from your time with the Bejeweled Conclave.

Using This Faction.name: Using This Faction
Using This Faction.text:
As well-connected spies and secret keepers, members of the Bejeweled Conclave can provide characters with useful information. For example, the conclave might help the characters if they’ve lost a lead or are having trouble gaining access to an important public figure. The conclave might insist on a favor or secret in return, pulling the characters into its webs of intrigue.

The style of the Bejeweled Conclave involves elegance, manners, and class: all techniques to be admired. Just beware members’ hidden agendas.

Bejeweled Conclave.name: Bejeweled Conclave
Bejeweled Conclave.text:
The Bejeweled Conclave is known as an organization of professional entertainers and mediators who cater to wealthy clients. They host glamorous parties, serve as courtiers, broker deals, and provide entertainment for exclusive functions.

But the Bejeweled Conclave wields far more influence than its publicly known services indicate. Consummate agents behind the throne, the enchanters of the Bejeweled Conclave cultivate elite connections and shift the balance of power in cities across the world.

Bringers of Cosmic Dawn.name: 寰宇黎明使徒會
Bringers of Cosmic Dawn.text:
A secretive organization of amoral transmuters, the Bringers of Cosmic Dawn receives abstruse directives from alien entities that hail from the dark spaces between stars. Faction members magically mutate plants and creatures in preparation for visitation by these beings—an event they believe is inevitable. They believe these entities will witness their glorious transmutations, be impressed, and bring about an exalted future full of mutated aberrations that serve transmuters’ every whim.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.book.JournalEntry.aunArtHandoutsG2.JournalEntryPage.Xe1ypGrOaBxaLGhy classes=overlay-caption cite=false]

Goals and Activities.name: Goals and Activities
Goals and Activities.text:
The exact goals of the Bringers of Cosmic Dawn are inscrutable to many members, though all believe they are helping to usher an ascended age of existence. The faction draws unprincipled transmuters, fringe scientists, and irrational astronomers to its academy and observatory, the Cosmic Oculus, where they receive fractured instructions from the faction’s five leaders, known as the Starspeakers.

These communications have a consistent message: Faction members must transmute the flora and fauna surrounding the Cosmic Oculus. Invariably, this involves transforming plants into hostile, flesh-eating specimens and mutating beasts to rearrange organs, add joints to limbs, and cause them to secrete slime. In doing so, the faction hopes to gain the attention of alien entities they believe will descend and warp all worlds in their path.

The faction members are united in purpose but not in execution. Some pursue their own theories of mutation and transfiguration, experimenting on themselves as much as on other subjects. Some instructions communicated by the Starspeakers conflict with others, as though the alien entities they seek to communicate with weren’t working in concert. These contradictions mean that the faction’s work advances erratically, with rejected experiments as common as transformations deemed to be in concordance with the aliens’ will.

Dawnrise Canyon

Bringers of Cosmic Dawn members carry out most transmutations far from public scrutiny. The faction is based in the secluded Dawnrise Canyon, far below the clifftop where the Cosmic Oculus stands. The once-tranquil canyon is now a dangerous valley of frightening creatures, hostile plants, aggressive transmuters, and wandering aberrations drawn to the unnatural landscape. Time moves erratically in the region thanks to frequent use of time-altering magic to speed up or slow down specific mutations.

Opposition to the Far Realm

While outsiders might not comprehend the distinction between the alien intelligences the Starspeakers commune with and the monsters of the Far Realm, Bringers of Cosmic Dawn members fear and reject the Far Realm as unknowable, indescribable, and inimical to life. The faction works to counter Far Realm incursions and expels any members who deal directly with that domain of incomprehensible horror.

Leadership and Organization.name: Leadership and Organization
Leadership and Organization.text:
The Bringers of the Cosmic Dawn lacks a rigid hierarchy, but its leaders maintain careful control over the information they receive from both members’ experiments and alien intelligences.

Member Roles

Certain members of the Bringers of Cosmic Dawn have special roles in the faction.

Starspeakers. The five enigmatic Starspeakers command the entire faction. None answer to any name besides their title, and they rarely leave the Cosmic Oculus except to measure progress within Dawnrise Canyon. Four Starspeakers (Medium @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmAberrantCultis]{Aberrant Cultists}) are human. The fifth and most senior Starspeaker appears to be an elderly human astronomer, but she is actually a magically disguised @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmAboleth0000000]{Aboleth} who has eschewed the Far Realm.

Worldwarpers. Most faction members work at the Cosmic Oculus or Dawnrise Canyon, but others, called Worldwarpers, venture into civilized lands to engage in more far-flung experimentation. Worldwarpers seek out willing recipients to, as they put it, “gain blessings from beyond the stars.”

Worldwarpers might offer to improve a banker’s garden with voracious plants to deter thieves, provide an aberration to help guard a prison, or augment a diplomat’s body to produce intoxicating pheromones. Like the work in Dawnrise Canyon, these puzzling changes ostensibly further a wider agenda, but Worldwarpers are rarely aware of the end goals; they merely put pieces in place as commanded and report back to the Starspeakers.

Blots. The Starspeakers secretly assign faction members to find and eradicate Far Realm sympathizers. These individuals, known within the faction as Blots, also venture into places where the Far Realm’s stain bleeds into the world, seeking to quash the Far Realm’s presence wherever they find it.

Things Beyond the Stars

The Bringers of Cosmic Dawn receive messages from many alien intelligences, not all of which are aligned with one another. You can use the Alien Entities table to generate sample intelligences that are directing the Bringers of Cosmic Dawn.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.tables.RollTable.aunAlienEntitiZA rollable resultLabel="Entity" captionPosition=top]{Alien Entities}

Joining the Bringers

Transmuters might seek out the Bringers of Cosmic Dawn even if they don’t wish to advance the faction’s goals. Faction members are undeniable masters of Transmutation magic, and some daring characters might join long enough to learn their secrets. Although some transmuters escape the faction, far too many begin to believe the Starspeakers’ ramblings and become devotees—or worse, they become unwilling subjects for experimental mutations when their disloyalty is uncovered.

Cosmic Oculus

Once an abandoned observatory, the Cosmic Oculus became the Bringers of Cosmic Dawn’s base when the faction discovered that the facility seems to magically amplify the messages of entities between the stars. In addition to the Starspeakers, faction astronomers also live in the Cosmic Oculus to record psychic signals from deep space and make nightly measurements of celestial bodies.

Most faction members never see the inside of the Cosmic Oculus. The ramshackle buildings clustered along the cliff face between the observatory and the canyon have expanded and mutated on their own, and members have used spells such as Stone Shape and Fabricate to haphazardly extend walls, enclose laboratories, and create passageways through the rock.

The multiverse is vast and full of entities you can’t imagine. I judge not those who seek guidance from the stars—though if innocents come to harm, these experimenters will regret their choices.

Bringers of Cosmic Dawn Characters.name: Bringers of Cosmic Dawn Characters
Bringers of Cosmic Dawn Characters.text:
Most members of the Bringers of Cosmic Dawn are transmutation-focused mages, but any characters with an interest in astronomy, aberrations, or warping life are welcome. New recruits aren’t permitted to balk at the faction’s creations or goals.

The most welcome recruits are @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.classes.Item.phbscrSorcerer00]{Sorcerers} (especially those with the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.classes.Item.phbscrAberrantSo]{Aberrant Sorcery} subclass), @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.classes.Item.phbwlkWarlock000]{Warlocks} (especially those with the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.classes.Item.phbwlkGreatOldOn]{Great Old One Patron} subclass), or @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.classes.Item.phbwzdWizard0000]{Wizards} (especially those with the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.subclasses.Item.aunTransmuter000]{Transmuter} subclass; see chapter 1). Characters with proficiency in Arcana, Medicine, or Nature or with Navigator’s Tools are also valued as recruits, as are characters with the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.backgrounds.Item.aunCosmicDawnEO8]{Cosmic Dawn Experiment} (see chapter 1), @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.origins.Item.phbbgGuide000000]{Guide}, or @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.origins.Item.phbbgHermit00000]{Hermit} background.

Member Benefits

If you’re a member of the Bringers of Cosmic Dawn, you receive these benefits.

Starwatcher Gear. The Bringers of Cosmic Dawn provide you with @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.equipment.Item.phbtulNavigators]{Navigator’s Tools} and a blank notebook in which to record your astronomical observations.

Trinket. Roll on the Bringers of Cosmic Dawn Trinkets table to determine what trinket you have from your time with the Bringers of Cosmic Dawn.

Using This Faction.name: Using This Faction
Using This Faction.text:
The Bringers of Cosmic Dawn can easily serve as a villainous or amoral organization in your campaign. If the characters pursue villains to the Celestial Oculus, you can determine whether the Bringers of Cosmic Dawn fight the characters with the aid of powerful Transmutation magic and strange Aberrations, or if they turn out to be curious intellectuals duped by malign influences.

However, the Bringers of Cosmic Dawn need not be villains. The characters might need the faction’s extensive knowledge of Transmutation magic to undo a shape-shifting curse or restore a transmuted ally to the proper form. Members’ whispers about creatures from the depths of space might presage an incursion by conquering githyanki astride dragons or a fleet of mind flayers on spelljamming vessels.

Outline Your World.name: Outline Your World
Outline Your World.text:
@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.book.JournalEntry.aunArtHandoutsG2.JournalEntryPage.dJqlIvmM2hYgLsCk classes=overlay-caption cite=false]

Before you create individual realms and societies, determine basic details about magic in your world. Consider which categories of magic are most or least prevalent, how that magic shaped the world’s geography, and the nature of the major realms.

Categories of Magic

In the worlds of D&D, magic can be categorized in three main ways: by different approaches (arcane or divine), by the schools of magic, and by distinct magical traditions. You might use any of these categories to define the role of magic in your world.

Approaches to Magic. The spells of Bards, Sorcerers, Warlocks, and Wizards are commonly called arcane magic. These practitioners rely on direct apprehension of the laws and principles of magic. Wizards study those principles directly, Sorcerers and Bards have a more intuitive understanding, and Warlocks gain that knowledge through their pacts.

The spells of Clerics, Druids, Paladins, and Rangers are called divine magic, though the nature magic of Druids and Rangers is sometimes divided into its own category: primal magic. All these practitioners approach magic mediated by gods, the forces of nature, the sacred weight of a Paladin’s oath, or some other divine force.

Schools of Magic. The eight schools of magic are Abjuration, Conjuration, Divination, Enchantment, Evocation, Illusion, Necromancy, and Transmutation. These schools represent the underpinnings of all magic in a D&D world. All D&D spells belong to one of these schools.

In your world, spellcasters might experience sensory effects when casting spells of different schools. For example, their scalps might tingle while casting Evocation spells, they might see flashes of events in their peripheral vision while casting Divination spells, or they might smell the phantom scent of grave soil while casting Necromancy spells.

Magical Traditions. Spellcasters of any sort might practice a wide variety of magical traditions. Dragons claim to be the originators of magic on some worlds. Some magical traditions rely entirely on rituals (which characters can access through the Ritual Caster feat in the Player’s Handbook). Rune magic (discussed in Bigby Presents: Glory of the Giants) was pioneered by giants and represents a distinct magical tradition. In the Forgotten Realms setting, ancient elves developed the tradition of high magic and used it to transform the world. Spellcasters in that setting also developed the practice of Circle magic (detailed in Forgotten Realms: Heroes of Faerûn), which allows spellcasters to pool their efforts to cast powerful spells. Magical traditions can also be passed down through family lines, as is the case with Eberron’s dragonmarks—magical birthmarks that grant the use of specific spells (as described in Eberron: Forge of the Artificer).

Magical Geography

Think about the ways magic has shaped the physical landscape of your world. Perhaps a powerful archmage, desiring privacy, used magic to raise mountains around her home. Or a nation governed by powerful mages might cloak the realm in protective magic to block its enemies’ magical prying. Your world might boast enormous monuments or strange geographical features created by magic in eons long gone or left behind by the gods in an ancient war.

Magic can have more modest effects too, which nonetheless impact the daily life of your world’s residents. For example, in Calimport in the Forgotten Realms, a magical lake inside the city supplies water for residents, while a floating tower serves as headquarters for soldiers who ride flying carpets. The more common magic is in your setting, the more visible its effects should be throughout the world.

Magical Realms

As you think about your world’s geography, consider the realms within it. Are they all home to powerful spellcasters? Are some more reliant on magic than others?

Your world might include three realms that each rely on a different type of magic. For example, one realm is ruled by wizards who each focus on a particular school of magic. In contrast, another realm is the domain of warlocks who gain their powers from a mysterious, otherworldly entity, while the third realm is ruled by sorcerers who descend from dragons and those who worshipped them. This emphasis on different kinds of spellcasting in each realm gives each a distinct flavor and culture.

On the other hand, you might find it useful to have realms in your world that don’t emphasize magic to serve as a contrast to the realms that do. A small realm surrounded by warlike neighbors with large armies of ordinary soldiers, for example, might turn to magic to defend itself and become a haven for mages.

Attitudes Toward Magic.name: Attitudes Toward Magic
Attitudes Toward Magic.text:
Once you’ve determined the types of magic that pervade your world, consider how your world’s inhabitants view magic. Do they welcome magic and the potential it represents? Or do they resent and fear magic, seeing it as a force for unexpected change and danger? Do attitudes vary by region?

Trust in or Distrust of Magic

A society that has relied on magic for generations has likely grown accustomed to magic’s effects on daily life. Such societies’ traditions and practices take magic into account. If access to the Find Familiar spell is common, for example, public spaces and businesses would be designed to accommodate familiars as well as people.

Alternatively, a society might distrust magic that’s not a part of daily life. Perhaps an unfamiliar kind of magic is blamed for a memorable tragedy, leading people to distrust that type of magic. For example, a realm that’s been invaded by an army of undead might prohibit necromancy even if the realm encourages other schools of magic.

Magical Shortcuts

Magic can often accomplish tasks more quickly and easily than is normally possible. While people in a magic-rich society easily accept the convenience and reliability of magical substitutes for common services, there might be a backlash effect or unusual side effects from folk taking magic for granted.

For example, wealthy nobles might seek out a chef capable of making food “the old-fashioned way.” Or a society rife with healing magic might become obsessed with thrill-seeking and dangerous sports.

Religion.name: Religion
Religion.text:
Most D&D worlds have many gods, and a magical society usually has at least one god of magic.

Are there gods of magic in your world? Who are they? What do they expect of their worshippers and from individuals who wield magic? Are they benevolent, antagonistic, or ambivalent toward mortals?

Benevolent Magic Gods

You might include a benevolent god of magic in your world. Such a god believes magic should be used for good, improving the lives of ordinary people. They encourage teaching and promoting the use of magic, and aspiring mages are expected to maintain a moral and ethical code that emphasizes selflessness, duty, and charity.

For example, crafters in a world with a benevolent god of magic are encouraged to make Common magic items that benefit others. When adventurers recover lost magic from ancient dungeons, priests hide dangerous magic away while they share useful magic with as many people as possible.

Including a benevolent god of magic in your world doesn’t preclude the inclusion of evil mages. Indeed, a benevolent god of magic might be outnumbered or outmatched by evil rivals. This prompts the god of magic or their followers to seek help from the characters.

Mystra. Mystra is a benevolent god of magic in the Forgotten Realms setting. Mystra has been destroyed or defeated multiple times, but each time she has returned in a new form with the help of brave adventurers.

Antagonistic Magic Gods

A god of magic might spread evil, cruelty, and tyranny through the use of magic. An antagonistic god of magic favors nefarious uses of magic. Such a god’s necromancer followers might raise large armies of undead to unleash on the population. Or adherents might use powerful Evocation spells to destroy rival cities and those who live in them. An antagonistic god of magic might rule a realm dedicated to evil and populated with undead, devils or demons, and other bloodthirsty creatures.

Iuz and Vecna. The demigod Iuz, described in the Dungeon Master’s Guide, and Vecna, whose schemes to amass ultimate power are described in Vecna: Eve of Ruin, are both antagonistic gods who seek conquest through magic. Iuz is primarily a god of deceit and oppression, but his methods involve seeking ancient magic he can use to increase his power. Vecna plots from the shadows and reveals himself only when victory is nigh.

Ambivalent Magic Gods

A god of magic might be ambivalent about their followers. Such a deity cares more about whether magic is used than about how it is used. When characters recover lost magical secrets during an adventure, an ambivalent god of magic might want those magical secrets locked away and preserved—not out of a selfish desire to control the information, but out of an intellectual interest in ensuring this knowledge isn’t lost again.

Mystral. An ambivalent god of magic might guard the source of all magic or even embody magic. Mystral, the original god of magic in the Forgotten Realms, embodied magic in this way. When Mystral died, magic was transformed; spellcasting became unreliable, and spellcasters lost their ability to cast their most powerful spells. Magic stabilized only when the god of magic returned as Mystra.

Boccob. An ambivalent god of magic in the Greyhawk setting and patron of the legendary mage Mordenkainen, Boccob works to ensure that good and evil forces remain equal.

Weaving a Divine Tapestry

A high-magic setting might include multiple gods of magic, each with conflicting goals and methods. No single god is likely to completely satisfy a society ruled by mages where spellcasting is common. Including multiple competing gods of magic gives your players more choices for patron gods for their characters. The conflict between rival gods of magic can create adventures and drive campaigns.

Your world might have different gods for each school of magic (a god of Conjuration, for example, and a god of Transmutation). Or a primary god of magic might be assisted by other gods, each with their own emphasis. For example, Mystra is assisted by Azuth, a god of wizardry who is ambivalent in his outlook and uninterested in the moral and ethical use of magic.

Your world might even have no god focused entirely on magic. In a world where magic suffuses every aspect of life, every god might carry some responsibility for the use of magic as it impacts the rest of their portfolio. A god of war cares not just about weapons and bloodshed, but about the use of magic in battle. A god of crafting might have dominion over making magic items and over artisans who use magic in their trades. And a god of knowledge might govern the academic study of magic often associated with gods of magic. Eberron’s pantheon is a good example.

Technology.name: Technology
Technology.text:
Many D&D campaigns assume the technology of a medieval or early renaissance setting. However, the Dungeon Master’s Guide has rules for modern firearms and futuristic weapons such as Antimatter Rifles and Laser Pistols. Further examples of futuristic technology can be found in Quests from the Infinite Staircase.

When you create your magical world, consider what level of technology is present. Does advanced technology exist in your setting? If it does, what do people think of it? Is technology a replacement for or a supplement to magic?

Technological Revolution

To introduce more advanced technology into your world, you can present it as originating in a recent technological revolution. An ancient and magic-focused realm ruled by mages might suddenly discover technological innovation. This could streamline daily life with simple technology, such as long-range communications, and add options for characters who like technology. It could also threaten the realm’s rulers and therefore lead to technology being heavily regulated. Threatened rulers might hunt down inventors and destroy their creations. On the flip side, rulers might feel threatened by magic-users, leading these rulers to embrace technology to stave off power-hungry mages.

Rival Powers

Alternatively, you can introduce technology to your world by creating a rival realm that relies on technology much like your magical society relies on magic. These two realms could be equivalent in wealth, status, and influence, but what one accomplishes with spells, the other achieves through machines.

Consider whether characters might come from either realm, or if the entire party hails from one society or the other. The first case encourages wildly different characters; some heroes enter battle with the Magic Missile and Fireball spells prepared, while others rely on their trusty Laser Pistols and Grenade Launchers.

If all characters come from one of the realms, the other society can serve as a rival and antagonist. If, for example, all your characters are from a magical society bordering a high-technology realm, tension between these two lands runs high and conflict is inevitable. Your campaign might begin with the characters infiltrating their technologically advanced neighbor while concealing their magical skills. There, the characters discover a plan for a mechanical army to invade the party’s homeland. To thwart this invasion, the characters need to lead a force of conjured creatures, undead, and other magical warriors.

Magic and Technology in Tandem

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.book.JournalEntry.aunArtHandoutsG2.JournalEntryPage.MzDNZ6EkGc0N7cHH classes=overlay-caption cite=false]

Magic and technology need not be oppositional forces. You can create a society in which magic and technology operate side by side. In such a realm, bandits are just as likely to cast the Fire Bolt spell as they are to draw a Laser Pistol. Citizens predict the weather with the Druidcraft spell, but they tell time using a clock in the middle of town.

Eberron. In a variant of this approach, magic provides the power for technology. Magic is used this way in Eberron. Eberron has airships, trains, and other examples of industrial technology, but these devices are powered by spells, magic items, and Elementals instead of nonmagical batteries and engines. Instantaneous, long-distance communication is possible in Eberron through Sending Stones staffed by members of a dragonmarked house; the result is akin to a magical telegraph network. Similarly, the residents of your society might have access to magic items that duplicate the effects of phones, automobiles, and similar modern conveniences.

Laws.name: Laws
Laws.text:
Even a novice spellcaster, able to cast nothing more than a cantrip, can use their magic to kill. Powerful mages can secretly observe individuals from afar, probe the thoughts of others, or control minds. It stands to reason that magical societies would impose laws to restrict the use of invasive, coercive, and destructive magic.

When creating your magical world, consider how the law restricts the use of magic, if at all. Are mages punished only when their magic hurts others? Are certain spells always restricted, or does anything go?

Outlawed Magic

The simplest magic law is the strictest: a ban on all magic. Laws like this come about because a society has a long history of conflict with magical enemies, because magic is blamed for environmental or social ills, or because of simple superstition. Power-hungry mages who run a society might outlaw the use of magic by anyone other than the ruling class.

Vilhon Reach. Several regions of the Vilhon Reach in the Forgotten Realms curtail or ban magic, particularly magic used to charm or injure others.

Focusing on the Crime

Some magical societies consider laws against the use of magic unnecessary when existing laws already prohibit the harmful effects of magic. After all, murder is murder, whether the victim was killed with a sword, a spell, or the killer’s bare hands.

For example, a large city like Greyhawk or Waterdeep might have laws against theft and laws that prohibit spying on a person in their home. An individual caught performing such acts would be guilty of a crime whether they cast the Invisibility spell or used nonmagical means.

Magic might count as an aggravating factor during sentencing, however. An individual found guilty of murder who killed the victim with the Finger of Death spell might be given a harsher sentence by a judge.

Frontier Justice

In remote regions that lack effective law enforcement, individuals and communities decide how magic and mages are treated. Residents might be suspicious of magic and intolerant of public spellcasting. Or they might become antagonistic toward mages who use magic in a way the residents don’t like. As a third option, a single law enforcement official, such as a sheriff or marshal, might decide which mages are allowed to practice their craft undisturbed and which are driven out of town.

Ten-Towns. In the remote settlements of Ten-Towns in the Forgotten Realms, an innkeeper might hang up a “No Spells Allowed” sign and hire a bouncer or two to enforce this rule. Putting up such a sign is the innkeeper’s right, but the town guard (if there is a town guard) is under no obligation to enforce it.

Commerce.name: Commerce
Commerce.text:
@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.book.JournalEntry.aunArtHandoutsG2.JournalEntryPage.KYdk5yW46rGdRAHy classes="float-right overlay-caption" cite=false]

How magic intertwines with commerce in your world is a key part of how your characters interact with it.

How easily can your characters find magic item shops or mages to purchase spellcasting services from? How accessible are magic items of higher rarity, such as Legendary magic items or Artifacts? Do mages’ guilds regulate the accessibility of magic?

Magic Item Shops

While Spell Scrolls and Potions of Healing are included in gear a character can buy in the Player’s Handbook, the Dungeon Master’s Guide leaves it up to the DM to decide what magic items are available to purchase in a campaign. A variety of magic item shops might be common in your world.

If you want Rare or rarer magic items to feel special, treat them like antiquities or fine art. A magic item shop in such a setting could be owned and operated by a single person who has deep knowledge of magical lore and contacts all over the world. When an adventurer asks for a specific magic item, the shop owner can procure it eventually, but the search takes time and leads to an adventure.

If magic items are more common in your world, a magic item shop in a city might look more like a pawnshop. All kinds of magic items would line the shelves, including duplicates of especially useful items such as Bags of Holding. The owner might be assisted by several individuals who specialize in security and deterring theft.

Magical Businesses

While any mage can sell their spellcasting services, your magical society might be filled with mages who use magic to earn a living in more interesting ways. The Player’s Handbook presents availability and cost details for spellcasting services, but you can alter this availability as best suits your world.

For example, a novice spellcaster who can cast the Prestidigitation spell could operate a laundry service, quickly and easily cleaning clothes. A chef could use the same spell to flavor food for an hour. Cantrips such as Elementalism, Guidance, Mending, and Spare the Dying are also well suited for a humble but reliable magical career.

Magical businesses could take dramatic forms in your setting. Eberron is full of examples, from the magical artificers of House Cannith to the magical bodyguards of House Deneith.

Mages’ Guilds

A mages’ guild is an alliance of mages who run a robust magical business in a city. Such guilds are a staple of fantasy roleplaying games, especially campaigns with roots in D&D’s earliest editions and settings, such as Greyhawk.

Guild Practices. A successful mages’ guild works hand in hand with the local law enforcement. Typically, local laws don’t prohibit spellcasting or making magic items, but they prohibit those who don’t belong to the guild from making a profit by providing services that fall under the guild’s exclusive concerns.

The local law enforcement typically includes members who are mages—and members of the guild. Both the guild and law enforcement tend to spend considerable time and effort monitoring mages in the city, enforcing guild rules and looking for mages avoiding guild membership.

Membership. Mages in a guild enjoy a monopoly on magical commerce. They expect to be paid an agreed-on amount of money for their services. Further, the guild is an excellent place for networking with other mages, and it probably operates a guildhall that includes a library of magical tomes and spellbooks as well as dining facilities, sleeping areas, and more. A guildhall could serve as an excellent base of operations for a group of characters connected to the guild.

Guild members are expected to pay dues and obey the guild’s rules. In this way, a mages’ guild in your world could serve as your characters’ employer—as well as their debt holder.

Rank. Membership in the guild might be structured into three or more ranks. While members of the lowest rank have no influence in the guild and are expected to assist senior members for little or no pay, high-ranking members enjoy a wealthy lifestyle, authority in the guild, and the assistance of lower-ranking members.

Campaign Role. A mages’ guild can serve as a group patron for characters or as an adversary that must be overcome. As a patron, the guild offers access to spellbooks, a comfortable refuge from danger, and magical allies knowledgeable on numerous subjects.

But a mages’ guild might instead be an oppressive organization that ruthlessly exploits its monopoly and harasses nonmembers. Your campaign could focus on ousting the guild’s leaders and replacing them with egalitarian leadership.

Magical Armies.name: Magical Armies
Magical Armies.text:
Fantasy realms raise and maintain armies to defend their territories. A society steeped in magic might establish magical armies to complement its regular troops. What benefits do magical armies provide, and what forms do they take?

War Wizards

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.book.JournalEntry.aunArtHandoutsG2.JournalEntryPage.ul9h5wqwOkHwbxVr classes="float-right overlay-caption" cite=false]

A magical army might boast mages in its ranks, either mixed in among ordinary soldiers or forming elite units composed entirely of spellcasters. The War Wizards of Cormyr in the Forgotten Realms is an archetypal example of this kind of elite unit.

War wizards defy mage stereotypes. They often wear armor and wield martial weapons, resembling Eldritch Knights. Alternatively, a war wizard might wear simple robes and wield a staff but focus on damaging spells. These mages function as mobile artillery units, protected by martial soldiers. Spellguards (see chapter 6) might feature prominently in such an army.

Magical Minions

A magical army might supplement or even replace ordinary soldiers with magical minions. During the Last War, Eberron’s armies extensively used magical minions, with the nation of Karrnath fielding armies of zombies and skeletons while Cyre and other nations used constructs. Outside Eberron, other magical realms fill their armies with conjured creatures or elementals summoned from the Inner Planes.

Fielding magical minions allows commanders and martial soldiers to remain safely behind the battle line while the minions participate in combat. A realm heavily dependent on magical minions might enter war more quickly than other realms and take more risks on the battlefield, brushing off the loss of magical minions as insignificant since they’re easily replaced.

Magical Fortifications

A traditional castle isn’t much of a defense against mages who can cast spells such as Fly, Passwall, and Teleport. Fortunately, a realm with magical resources has many magical ways to defend itself. Defensive measures such as the Wall of Force, Globe of Invulnerability, and Antimagic Field spells cover a small area for a limited time and are useful in emergencies. But options such as the Forbiddance and Guards and Wards spells last much longer and can provide layers of magical defenses. Entrances can be protected with the Glyph of Warding spell.

A fortification might be protected by magical defenders that negate an enemy’s advantages. For example, flying assailants could be countered with flying defenders, such as soldiers mounted on griffins, hippogriffs, or pegasi.

Mastering Magic.name: Mastering Magic
Mastering Magic.text:
If magic suffuses your world, consider how its inhabitants learn their magical craft. Is magic laboriously taught by an elderly expert to a single apprentice? Do aspiring mages enroll at an academy where they’re taught alongside others? Or do novice spellcasters learn another way?

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.book.JournalEntry.aunArtHandoutsG2.JournalEntryPage.EOzzB5fWblSbAHzK classes=overlay-caption cite=false]

The forms of magical instruction can be described in four ways: solitary study, apprenticeship, academic instruction, or cultural immersion, where magical instruction is readily available to all. Most magical societies rely on a single type of magical instruction. You might decide, however, that different kinds of instruction are prevalent in different parts of the world. For example, a magical realm might boast a magical academy with hundreds of students, but in the realm’s capital, magic might be so common that everyone knows a spell or two thanks to the cultural prevalence of magic in everyday life.

Solitary Study

When magic is learned through solitary study, each mage understands magic slightly differently. For example, one mage might conceive of magic as influenced by the stars and planets, while another conceptualizes magic as an imperceptible force that connects all things. Both mages can cast spells of equivalent strength and effect, but their understanding of the underlying origin of magic varies.

Warlocks. In a society that relies on solitary study, every mage is self-taught. Warlocks, who cobble together magical power from pacts and little-understood scraps of lore, are the most common kind of spellcaster in these societies. Wizards, who traditionally rely on learning from others, might be rare.

Apprenticeship

When magic is learned through apprenticeship, magical instruction is limited to one-on-one relationships between an expert and a novice. An experienced mage might have many apprentices in a lifetime but teach only one at a time. As a result, there are always more candidates for apprenticeship than mentors, and competition among potential apprentices might be intense. Experienced mages might screen candidates or develop elaborate tests for prospective apprentices, measuring their intelligence, loyalty, magical acumen, or ethical code. These tests might serve as low-level adventures in your world.

Campaigns. In a campaign focused on apprenticeship, the mentor becomes unusually important. Craft interesting mentors your players will enjoy interacting with. The archetypal mentor is enigmatic and seemingly omnipotent, but they can also be whimsical, grouchy, or absent-minded.

In addition to creating a memorable mentor, consider when and how your characters’ apprenticeships end. Is a level 1 Wizard finished with their apprenticeship? Or do they remain an apprentice until level 3 or later? How does the mentor decide when the student has learned enough?

Sorcerers. Sorcerers flourish in societies focused on apprenticeship. Many sorcerers inherit their powers from a magical ancestor, or their powers might be shared among members of their family. These family connections make it easier to secure a mentor, and the family might have well-established traditions around recognizing, controlling, and mastering magic.

Academic Instruction

In a long-established magical society, the myriad magical philosophies taught by individual mentors eventually coalesce around the most successful teachers. When these teachers pool their resources to form a magical academy, large numbers of students can benefit from academic instruction. Styles of magical academies are further detailed in “Magical Academies” below.

Wizards. Wizards flourish in a magical society with academic instruction. Dutifully showing up to school every day, books in hand, Wizards learn new spells in a classroom environment. During off hours, they practice magic, pursue magical interests on their own, and get into the sort of trouble students always find.

Cultural Immersion

Magic in your society might be so well understood and so widespread that aspiring mages can learn basic magic from everyday life. In such a society, books of magical instruction might be found at any bookstore or library. Everyone might know a spell or two, and learning a new one might be as easy as sitting down for a few hours with a friend and exchanging techniques. When magic is widely understood and a part of everyday life, you don’t need to create magical academies or mentor figures to explain why characters know basic magic.

Bards. Bards—whose magic takes the form of music, dance, and other popular art forms—flourish in a society where magic is popular. To Bards, learning new magic might be as simple as overhearing a catchy tune in a tavern and reworking it for their own purposes.

Magical Academies

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.book.JournalEntry.aunArtHandoutsG2.JournalEntryPage.jfNotMUXXRAGWMBb classes=overlay-caption cite=false]

The magical academies in the worlds of D&D make useful models for your world-building. Consider the following when creating your magical academy.

Everything Under One Roof. The most common form of magical academy is a single place where several kinds of magic are taught. For example, Strixhaven, detailed in Strixhaven: A Curriculum of Chaos, is a magical academy where five different campuses teach opposing magic philosophies. Similarly, the Tower of High Sorcery in the Dragonlance setting, described in Dragonlance: Shadow of the Dragon Queen, teaches that setting’s three primary orders of magic.

An academy of this sort is home to mages with different philosophies, goals, and methods. These individuals are united around the higher goal of teaching magic to the next generation of students. A student at one of these academies has access to a wide variety of spells, magical traditions, and instructors. Because students come from far away, they benefit from interacting with people from all over the world.

This kind of academy provides players with a lot of character creation options. Characters of any background, species, class, or subclass might come together to study magic and are sent on adventures by teachers with competing agendas. A magical academy is an example of an esoteric institution group patron, detailed later in this chapter.

Rival Academies. A realm with a large population of aspiring mages might have multiple magical academies that each specialize in a different form of magic.

An academy of this sort might focus on a single kind of magic: for instance, magic from the Conjuration school, or bladesinging, an ancient elven technique of magical combat. Rivalries between such academies take forms ranging from athletic competitions to pranks, clandestine raids, or even physical violence.

Because all students at one such academy study a single kind of magic, the academy is less likely to function as the home base for your campaign. Instead, the rival academies likely feature in the backstories of characters who wield magic, serving as the source of the characters’ early magical training. However, you might create a campaign in which graduates of these rival academies are brought together by a menace that threatens all the academies or even the entire realm.

Building a Magical World.name: Building a Magical World
Building a Magical World.text:
The advice presented here will help you build your own magical world. Each of the sections that follow focuses on a different aspect of world-building, beginning with the broadest concepts and proceeding to specific topics, including questions designed to guide your creativity. Examples from throughout the D&D multiverse illustrate approaches to each of these subjects:

Outline Your World. Which types of magic and realms exist in your world?

Attitudes Toward Magic. How do people in your realms view magic and its use?

Religion. What gods of magic exist?

Technology. Does technology also exist, and if so, how do magic and technology interact?

Laws. Do laws regulate or encourage the use of magic?

Commerce. How does the business of spellcasting and magic items function, and are mages’ guilds prominent?

Magical Armies. How do the use and prevalence of magic affect warfare and the forces used to fight it?

Mastering Magic. How do mages learn magic, and what forms do magical academies take?

Magical worlds beyond the dreams of the most learned scholars hold limitless knowledge. Mystra willing, you might master their gifts. Use this power wisely, friends.

D&D Settings

Setting

Description

Sourcebook

Draconic magic is a major theme in this setting consumed by war. The use of magic granted by gods is rare.

Dragonlance: Shadow of the Dragon Queen

Magic is ubiquitous and functions like technology, providing services such as rapid transportation and long-distance communication.

Eberron: Forge of the Artificer and Eberron: Rising from the Last War

Forgotten Realms

Many types of magic infuse dozens of realms. The gods walk in disguise among mortals.

Forgotten Realms: Heroes of Faerûn and Forgotten Realms: Adventures in Faerûn

Greyhawk

Magic is widespread and commonly used but still wondrous and sometimes frightening.

Dungeon Master’s Guide

Ravenloft

Magical mists ensure each domain is a prison for its magical Darklord, or ruler, and the hapless residents here. Magic here is ominous and scary.

Character Options.name: Character Options
Character Options.text:
@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.book.JournalEntry.aunArtHandoutsG2.JournalEntryPage.LNQsrH9X4xuajIMD classes=overlay-caption cite=false]

This chapter is full of new character options you can use to make characters suited to magical settings. The pages that follow include new and revised subclasses, new backgrounds, and new feats.

Covenant of the Grave.name: Covenant of the Grave
Covenant of the Grave.text:
The Covenant of the Grave is a loose affiliation of necromancers and those interested in studying death and undeath through a disciplined, scientific lens. The covenant has no room for megalomaniacs who seek domination via hordes of undead minions.

These realists are aware that their studies, no matter how clinical, unnerve most people, so their members are unobtrusive and their laboratories hidden. The greatest covenant academy is the Pale Tower, a morbid, bone-white structure far from civilization.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.book.JournalEntry.aunArtHandoutsG2.JournalEntryPage.wyJ6zOXKMSF8M7Gf classes=overlay-caption cite=false]

Goals and Activities.name: Goals and Activities
Goals and Activities.text:
Covenant members are typically more interested in deepening their knowledge than their power. They freely share their research with each other via correspondence, personal visits, or clandestine lectures, but they rarely reveal discoveries to those outside the organization. Many worry that their research might be misused for sinister, nonacademic ends. Others simply don’t expect anyone but like-minded scholars to comprehend their work.

Unlike necromancers who incite undead uprisings, the Covenant of the Grave usually works to stymie undead hordes and return less powerful undead to the safer confines of the laboratory or grave. Members consider undead rampages dreadfully unscientific, if not outright embarrassing. They’re keenly aware of the harm that such villainous necromancy brings to the faction’s reputation. Their opposition to necromantic wickedness sometimes puts the faction in conflict with powerful undead such as liches, death knights, or vampires.

Leadership and Organization.name: Leadership and Organization
Leadership and Organization.text:
Although an established hierarchy exists within the Covenant of the Grave, members are usually too engrossed in their own research to worry about rank.

Necrodemics and Gravetenders

Any faction member who shares a significant scholarly truth about death, decay, or undeath with the faction might gain the title of Necrodemic. Some members hold expanded titles such as Arisen Necrodemic or Necrodemic Embalmist, awarded for sharing more complex knowledge.

The title of Gravetender is held by the three head administrators of the Pale Tower. Emeritus administrators keep this title after retirement, so four to six Gravetenders usually exist at a time. Gravetenders set the overall direction for the faction but are usually bookish and circumspect, so change within the faction is gradual.

Joining the Covenant

Any spellcaster with an interest in Necromancy magic or macabre research is likely to hear about the Covenant of the Grave, but the faction doesn’t actively recruit. The covenant expects aspirants to independently identify its members and present a well-reasoned proposal for membership. A member who receives a qualified aspirant usually confers with other members before either taking on the aspirant as a research assistant or sending them to study at the Pale Tower.

Undead Members

Only a few members of the Covenant of the Grave are undead. Covenant members have little use for less powerful undead such as skeletons and zombies, and other undead are usually too consumed by their hungers to maintain the intellectual rigor the covenant expects. The Undead Members table details the few undead scholars in the covenant.

Undead Members

Name

Description

Adlin Humbington

A bookish @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmGhost000000000]{Ghost} who haunts his surgical theater, Adlin is so tied to his experiments that he’s unaware he’s dead.

Kadra Faldrig

The Lawful Neutral @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmLich0000000000]{Lich} Kadra hides that she’s undead so her highly regarded insights into lichdom seem inspired by intellect rather than a study of her own nature.

Melodin the Risen

A determined @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmRevenant000000]{Revenant} , Melodin is a Gravetender of the Pale Tower who seeks to avenge herself against her predecessor by proving herself the superior administrator.

The Pale Tower

The greatest concentration of covenant members resides in the Pale Tower. Rising from a noxious swamp, this bone-white structure is thousands of years old. The tower’s small, dingy exterior belies its underground warren of classrooms, laboratories, and ossuaries.

In addition to being an academy and research institution, the Pale Tower is a repository of sinister necromantic magic that the covenant doesn’t want misused. Rumors hold that malicious artifacts, lost Necromancy spells, and soul-staining magic items are locked away in vaults only the Gravetenders can access.

Renown Rewards.name: Renown Rewards
Renown Rewards.text:
Characters gain renown with the Covenant of the Grave by sharing scholarly insights into death or undeath or by completing quests for the Covenant. As their Renown Scores increase, characters gain access to various perks, as shown on the Covenant of the Grave Renown table. If your campaign doesn’t use renown, the DM decides if and when characters earn these perks.

You always have the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.spells.Item.phbsplSpeakwithD]{Speak with Dead} spell prepared, and you can cast it once without expending a spell slot. You regain the ability to cast it in this way when you finish a Long Rest. Intelligence, Wisdom, or Charisma is your spellcasting ability for this spell (choose when you gain this reward). This reward is free the first time you use it. On subsequent occasions, you must provide any Material components normally consumed by the spell.

Covenant of the Grave Characters.name: Covenant of the Grave Characters
Covenant of the Grave Characters.text:
Joining the Covenant of the Grave is advantageous to any character interested in the secrets of life and death. While intellectual rigor is important, knowledge of any death-adjacent subject is sufficient for aspiring members.

The most welcome aspirants are @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.classes.Item.phbclcCleric0000]{Clerics}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.classes.Item.phbmnkMonk000000]{Monks}, and @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.classes.Item.phbwzdWizard0000]{Wizards} (especially those with the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.subclasses.Item.aunNecromancer00]{Necromancer} subclass; see chapter 1). Characters with proficiency in Arcana, Investigation, or Medicine; proficiency with @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.equipment.Item.phbtulLeatherwor]{Leatherworker’s Tools}; or the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.backgrounds.Item.aunCovenantofTRS]{Covenant of the Grave Recruit} (see chapter 1), @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.origins.Item.phbbgSage0000000]{Sage}, or @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.origins.Item.phbbgScribe00000]{Scribe} background are also good fits.

Member Benefits

If you’re a member of the Covenant of the Grave, you receive these benefits.

Grave Services. The covenant respectfully performs final rites for your corpse whenever the inevitable comes to pass.

Modest Lifestyle. The covenant pays you a stipend that supports your Modest lifestyle (1 GP per day).

Trinket. Roll on the Covenant of the Grave Trinkets table to determine what trinket you have from your time with the covenant.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.tables.RollTable.aunCovenantoftmE rollable resultLabel="Trinket" captionPosition=top]{Covenant of the Grave Trinkets}

Using This Faction.name: Using This Faction
Using This Faction.text:
Faction members might warn the characters of potential necromantic uprisings or escort the party through lands plagued with undead. Having access to graveyards and burial houses, the faction might also recover the corpse of someone the characters want to revive or question.

The covenant isn’t likely to aid the characters for free. Members might request lost necromantic lore in exchange for their help or task the party with defeating a necromancer or undead creature who has rejected the covenant’s academic overtures.

Necromancy isn’t inherently evil. It is those who defile the dead and manipulate the living who deserve our disapproval, not those who study life and death.

Creating Magical Worlds.name: Creating Magical Worlds
Creating Magical Worlds.text:
@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.book.JournalEntry.aunArtHandoutsG2.JournalEntryPage.wQwpDsyDKbAPpXtZ classes=overlay-caption cite=false]

Using the advice and tools in this chapter, you can create your own world infused with magic for your D&D games. This chapter also provides guidelines for tailoring a group patron for your characters’ adventures, helping the players feel immersed in your setting. When creating your magical world, you can choose the options you like best or modify an existing world using your favorite advice. For example, you could use an archmage group patron of your own creation in your adventures that take place in the Forgotten Realms.

Magic in Existing Worlds.name: Magic in Existing Worlds
Magic in Existing Worlds.text: If you want to use this chapter’s advice within an existing world, consider the ones on the D&D Settings table. It describes the magic prevalent in each setting as well as where you can find more information about those settings.

Crucible Keepers.name: Crucible Keepers
Crucible Keepers.text:
The Crucible Keepers consists of daredevil evokers who venture into natural or magical disasters to study the phenomenal power at play. Some members use their Evocation magic to counter disasters and help others, while other members revel in nature’s destructive forces and take inspiration from them to enhance their own devastating spellcraft.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.book.JournalEntry.aunArtHandoutsG2.JournalEntryPage.S2sAmD7Ae1PnWlh8 classes=overlay-caption cite=false]

Overuse of powerful evocation magic can warp the land as well as the souls of those who become drunk on magical power. The Crucible Keepers’ attempt to right these wrongs is noble.

Goals and Activities.name: Goals and Activities
Goals and Activities.text:
Crucible Keepers study Evocation magic to command energy and control powerful forces. They eschew solitary scholarship, preferring informal gatherings where they exchange ideas and try to impress their peers with spectacular displays of magical might.

Faction members might be thrill seekers, but they aren’t fools. They plan their dangerous endeavors well in advance, spending days or weeks charting natural or magical phenomena before enjoying the rush of soaring through the eye of a hurricane or surfing a lava flow. They employ protective magic while engaging in these endeavors, and they’re quick to chide fools who confront danger unprepared.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.book.JournalEntry.aunArtHandoutsG2.JournalEntryPage.fsZj90IomPE8FL8r classes=overlay-caption cite=false]

Leadership and Organization.name: Leadership and Organization
Leadership and Organization.text:
Those drawn to the Crucible Keepers aren’t the sort who like following orders. Ranks within the Crucible Keepers are unofficial, fluid, and based on frequent competitive challenges between members, with losers acknowledging winners’ higher rank. Challenges usually involve magical duels, elaborate races, or dangerous stunts.

Joining the Crucible Keepers

The Crucible Keepers enthusiastically welcomes anyone who wants to try out for its ranks. Gaining membership is as simple as impressing any faction member with a clever display of Evocation magic, a wild physical stunt, or a dramatic parlor trick.

Eljar Charscale

The current head of the Crucible Keepers is a dragonborn named Eljar Charscale (Medium @UUID[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.actors.Actor.aunEvokerArchmag]{Evoker Archmage}; see chapter 6). Originally a human, Eljar was executed by cruel generals when he refused to use his magic in an unpopular war. After his allies reincarnated him, Eljar fled in his new dragonborn body. He took the name Charscale on joining the Crucible Keepers.

Eljar loves the thrill of Evocation magic and is undefeated in duels of spellcraft. In addition to his magical talent, Eljar is respected for listening to everyone and offering sensible guidance. He began leading the Crucible Keepers only a few months ago after the former leader died in a forest fire.

Eljar has a strong antiwar stance that he disseminates throughout the organization. He has forbidden members of the Crucible Keepers from serving as military battle mages. Some evokers believe this stance restricts their career paths, but most understand the reasoning behind Eljar’s policy.

Disaster Chasers

Crucible Keepers predict and study natural and magical disasters, both to warn those who will be affected and to explore nature’s incredible power. You can roll on or choose a result from the Pending Disasters table to generate a sample disaster Crucible Keepers plan to address.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.tables.RollTable.aunPendingDisafr rollable resultLabel="Disaster" captionPosition=top]{Pending Disasters}

Caldera Arcadium

Although members believe that nature is the best classroom, the Crucible Keepers maintains a learning institution focused on Evocation magic. The Caldera Arcadium is a large stone building hanging over the rim of an active volcano, suspended by enormous metal chains and struts.

The temperature inside the building ranges from unpleasantly warm to blisteringly hot, but eager students fill its three classrooms every day. The building also holds magical forges for the study and creation of magic items. A stone bridge from the Arcadium’s roof leads to dormitories, academic offices, and a cafeteria, all hanging off the volcano’s edge.

The Caldera Arcadium’s headmaster is a scholarly @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmEfreeti0000000]{Efreeti} named Nadia Flameheart, who taught magic in the City of Brass for a millennium before joining the Crucible Keepers. The only wishes she entertains are those for better grades, and her only responses are tips for studying.

Fire-blackened @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmStoneGolem0000]{Stone Golems} called the Scorchborn provide security for the Arcadium, a duty that mostly involves defusing fights between hotheaded students. The Scorchborn are also instrumental to the wards that protect the school from volcanic eruptions, but not even Nadia Flameheart understands how. Since all Scorchborn are identical, no one is sure how many there are. No danger has yet presented a sufficient threat to marshal them all in one place.

Arcadium students frequently engage in death-defying stunts they call “field trips.” The most common stunt is a leap from an Arcadium balcony during an eruption, trusting an ordinary rope to prevent a fall into lava. Another popular field trip involves launching homemade hang gliders from the volcano’s edge.

Renown Rewards.name: Renown Rewards
Renown Rewards.text:
Characters gain renown with the Crucible Keepers by surviving natural disasters or by completing Crucible Keeper missions. As their Renown Scores increase, characters gain access to various perks, as shown on the Crucible Keepers Renown table. If your campaign doesn’t use renown, the DM decides if and when characters earn these perks.

A reckless @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmMageApprentice]{Mage Apprentice} becomes your loyal fan. You can order this apprentice to assist you for one mission. Once you use this reward, you can’t do so again until your Renown Score increases.

Once you use this reward, you can’t do so again until your Renown Score increases.

Crucible Keepers Characters.name: Crucible Keepers Characters
Crucible Keepers Characters.text:
The Crucible Keepers welcomes anyone willing to study destruction up close, which brings a high proportion of daredevils and thrill seekers into its ranks. Characters who are @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.classes.Item.phbbrbBarbarian0]{Barbarians}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.classes.Item.phbdrdDruid00000]{Druids}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.classes.Item.phbscrSorcerer00]{Sorcerers}, or @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.classes.Item.phbwzdWizard0000]{Wizards} (especially those with the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.classes.Item.phbwzdEvoker0000]{Evoker} subclass) are likely to be sought after as members, as are those with proficiency in Intimidation, Nature, or Survival or with the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.backgrounds.Item.aunCrucibleStoLm]{Crucible Storm Chaser} (see chapter 1) or @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.origins.Item.phbbgNoble000000]{Noble} background.

Member Benefits

If you’re a member of the Crucible Keepers, you receive these benefits.

Poor Lifestyle. The Crucible Keepers pays you a stipend that supports a Poor lifestyle (2 SP per day).

Trinket. Roll on the Crucible Keepers Trinkets table to determine what trinket you have from your time in the Crucible Keepers.
