Using This Faction.name: Using This Faction
Using This Faction.text:
Crucible Keepers are often harbingers of catastrophe. If they appear in large numbers, it’s usually because they anticipate an imminent disaster. A Crucible Keeper traveling through a dangerous area might hire the party to escort them, but it would be wise to ask what awaits at the journey’s end.

However, Crucible Keepers are evokers, not diviners, so their guesses are sometimes wrong. As the DM, you can decide whether that means the disaster doesn’t happen, is earlier or later by days, or is some other event entirely.

Crucible Keepers also study the aftermath of disasters, both natural and magical. Their presence might be a detriment or a blessing for recovery efforts. Unscrupulous members revel in disasters’ aftermath and might seek to profit from them, while selfless members work to ease suffering.

Most darkenbeasts have luminous bones that glow through their skin; they resemble eerie flying skeletons as they soar through the night sky. A darkenbeast is loyal to its creators, who can extract the magic used to transform it in a dramatic display that’s fatal to the darkenbeast.

When to Evolve Magic Items.name: When to Evolve Magic Items
When to Evolve Magic Items.text:
You decide when a magic item evolves. In general, a magic item evolves when a character’s power level increases to the next tier of play. Treat this as a guideline, not a rule.

Repeated Evolutions

You can evolve a magic item multiple times. Each time you evolve it, the magic item retains its properties from its previous rarity (or rarities) and gains a property from its new rarity.

You can evolve a magic item before or after awarding it to a character. In either case, you can increase the item’s rarity as the character gains power until its rarity becomes Legendary.

Crafting Evolution

You might also decide that characters can evolve their magic items using the rules for crafting magic items in the Dungeon Master’s Guide. If you allow this, the time required to evolve the item equals the difference between the time required to craft an item of the evolving item’s new rarity and the time required to craft an item of its previous rarity. Likewise, the cost required is the difference between the cost to craft an item of the evolving item’s new rarity and the cost to craft an item of its previous rarity. So evolving an Uncommon item (which requires 10 days and 200 GP to craft) into a Rare item (which requires 50 days and 2,000 GP to craft) requires 40 days and 1,800 GP in raw materials.

Results of Evolution.name: Results of Evolution
Results of Evolution.text:
This section describes the results of magic item evolution.

Name and Appearance

Each item’s name changes when it evolves, as noted for that type of evolving magic item. Its appearance also changes as it evolves.

Rarity

When a magic item evolves, its rarity increases to the next highest rarity: from Common to Uncommon, from Rare to Very Rare, and so forth. A Legendary magic item can’t evolve.

Attunement

A magic item keeps its Attunement requirement (or lack thereof) as it evolves. If a creature is attuned to a magic item when the item evolves, the creature retains its Attunement to that item.

Cumulative Abilities

When an evolving magic item evolves, it retains the properties described in its previous rarities and gains the properties described in its new rarity. If an evolving weapon grants a bonus to attack rolls and damage rolls, however, that bonus replaces any similar bonus granted by a lower rarity instead of being added to it. For instance, in “Ready-Made Evolving Magic Items,” a Keyholes Dagger’s bonus to attack and damage rolls is +1 when Uncommon, +2 when Rare, and +3 when Very Rare.

Ready-Made Evolving Magic Items.name: Ready-Made Evolving Magic Items
Ready-Made Evolving Magic Items.text:
The ready-made evolving magic items presented in this section and listed in the Ready-Made Evolving Magic Items table are special rewards. You might award a Ranger a Blossom Rod, for example, to reinforce the character’s connection with nature, gradually increasing the rod’s rarity to reward the Ranger for their heroics. Similarly, a Necromancer might receive a Staff of Skulls as a gift if their mentor works with the Covenant of the Grave magical faction (see chapter 4).

You can structure a campaign arc around one of these items—use it to point the characters toward adventures related to its narrative, similar to how you might use an Artifact.

Ready-Made Evolving Item Names

When referring to one of these items, use the word that corresponds with the item’s rarity before its name. For example, an Uncommon Blossom Rod is a Budding Blossom Rod, a Rare one is a Flowering Blossom Rod, and a Very Rare one is a Somniferous Blossom Rod.

Blossom Rod

Rod, Rarity Varies (Requires Attunement by a Spellcaster)

This rod is made of intertwined, living plant stems.

Budding (Uncommon). Multicolored leaves decorate the rod’s stems, and a few buds cluster near each end.

While you hold the rod, you can cast Druidcraft or Plant Growth (Overgrowth only) from it. Once the rod has been used to cast Plant Growth, it can’t be used to cast this spell again until the next dawn.

While you hold the rod, as a Magic action, you can rejuvenate nonmagical plants in a 5-foot Cube you can see within 15 feet of yourself. The rejuvenated plants remain verdant for 1d4 days, after which they grow or wither as normal plants would.

Flowering (Rare). Both ends of the rod bear colorful, fragrant flowers. While you hold the rod, you can cast Insect Plague from it, using your spell save DC. When you do so, the insects appear as bumblebees. Once the rod has been used to cast this spell, it can’t be used to cast this spell again until the next dawn.

Somniferous (Very Rare). Robust bursts of flowers grow along the rod’s length.

While you hold the rod, you can take a Magic action to expel a puff of sleep-inducing pollen in a 30-foot Emanation originating from you. Creatures of your choice in the Emanation must succeed on a DC 17 Constitution saving throw or have the Unconscious condition for 1 hour. Creatures that don’t sleep, such as elves, or that have Immunity to the Exhaustion condition automatically succeed on the save. The effect ends on a target if it takes damage or a creature within 5 feet of it takes an action to shake it awake. Once the rod has produced this effect, it can’t do so again until the next dawn.

This idol resembles an elephant sitting on its haunches, smiling regally behind its uplifted trunk.

Blemished (Uncommon). The idol is made of tarnished bronze, with minor dings and dents scattered over its surface.

You can cast the Augury spell from the idol. The idol speaks the omen aloud in response. Once the idol has been used to cast this spell, it can’t be used to cast this spell again until the next dawn.

Tarnished (Rare). The idol is made of gold, with a patina of dust settled into its crevices.

While attuned to the idol, you gain a +1 bonus to your Armor Class. Additionally, while holding the idol, you can take a Magic action to touch a nonmagical trade bar or gemstone. The item is then transformed into coinage equivalent to its value. For example, if you take a Magic action to touch a 5-pound silver bar while holding the idol, the bar is transformed into 25 GP worth of coins.

Golden (Very Rare). The idol is made of gleaming gold, and the elephant’s eyes are set with shining rubies.

While holding the idol, you can cast Globe of Invulnerability from it. Once the idol has been used to cast this spell, it can’t be used to cast this spell again until the next dawn.

It remains transformed in this way until the start of your next turn, at which point it reverts back to its Dagger form. Regardless of the weapon’s form, you can use your choice of your Strength or Dexterity modifier for the attack and damage rolls; you must use the same modifier for both rolls.

Ten (Rare). Ten ornamental keyholes adorn the weapon’s hilt. Your bonus to attack rolls and damage rolls made with this magic weapon increases to +2. Additionally, when you transform the weapon, you can now transform it into any Simple Melee weapon.

When you transform the weapon, you can now also transform it into a Battleaxe, Longsword, Rapier, Scimitar, or Warhammer.

Additionally, when you miss with an attack roll using this weapon, you can reroll the attack, potentially turning the miss into a hit. You must use the second roll. Once used, this property can’t be used again until the next dawn.

While you hold the staff, you can take a Magic action to point the staff at a Humanoid you can see. That creature makes a DC 17 Constitution saving throw. Complex Evolution Examples.name: Complex Evolution Examples
Complex Evolution Examples.text:
The following examples show how to apply the rules for complex evolution to magic items from the Dungeon Master’s Guide. These examples give fantastical new names to the base items and provide story details to show how you can use these elements to enhance your game.

When referring to one of these items, use the word that corresponds with the item’s rarity before its name. For example, a Rare Blade of the Guardian is a Studious Blade of the Guardian, a Very Rare one is a Resistant Blade of the Guardian, and a Legendary one is an All-Seeing Blade of the Guardian.

Blade of the Guardian

In this example, a Paladin finds a treasured Weapon of Warning (Greatsword), an Uncommon magic item, early in her adventuring career. Each time the weapon evolves, the shield patterns etched into its blade become more intricate.

Studious (Rare). The DM decides the weapon evolves to a Rare item and gives it the Studious property, since the Paladin has improved her investigative skills to better understand potential threats.

Resistant (Very Rare). When the Paladin defends her companions against infernal forces, the DM decides the weapon evolves again, becoming Very Rare and gaining the Resistant property. The DM chooses Fire as the damage type it grants Resistance to, since that’s thematically appropriate.

All-Seeing (Legendary). The DM decides the weapon evolves one final time, becoming Legendary and gaining the All-Seeing property. The DM decides this represents the Paladin becoming a paragon of watchful protection.

Breastplate of the Tyrant

In this example, a Fighter finds an Armor of Resistance (Breastplate) while raiding an old dungeon. The armor, a Rare magic item, grants Resistance to Psychic damage and bears the emblem of a barbed crown. Each time the armor evolves, the pattern of spikes around the crown grows more complex.

Regal (Very Rare). When the characters travel to an ancient battlefield, the DM decides the armor evolves, becoming Very Rare and gaining the Regal property. As the characters explore, they uncover iconography matching that on the armor.

Subjugating (Legendary). The characters’ investigation leads them to an old castle, where they face an ancient, brutal tyrant wearing a tabard with iconography matching this armor. The characters defeat the tyrant thanks to the Fighter’s heroics. The DM decides the armor evolves, becoming Legendary and gaining the Subjugating property.

Rod of the Honed Mind

In this example, a Warlock receives a +1 Rod of the Pact Keeper, an Uncommon magic item. The rod is a gift from a circle of sages who study the Warlock’s mysterious patron, an entity from beyond the stars. The rod bears abstruse symbols of unknown origin; each time it evolves, they become more intricate.

Vigilant (Rare). After discovering a strange tome full of symbols that match those on the rod, the Warlock feels the approval of the entity that fuels their magic. The DM decides the rod evolves and becomes Rare, gaining the Vigilant property.

Psionic (Very Rare). While exploring clues the Warlock deciphered from the strange tome, the characters acquire psionically charged crystals from the Underdark. The crystals bear the same symbols the rod has. The DM decides the rod evolves to become Very Rare, gaining the Psionic property.

Tranquil (Legendary). Thanks to the Warlock’s quick thinking, the characters defeat a band of cultists seeking to destroy anything connected to psionic magic. To reward the Warlock, the DM evolves the rod into its final form, making it Legendary and granting it the Tranquil property.

Wand of Celestial Prowess

In this example, a Cleric dedicated to a deity of the sky receives a +1 Wand of the War Mage, an Uncommon magic item, from his mentor. The ebony wand is simple but feels extraordinarily powerful when the Cleric touches it. Each time the wand evolves, carvings of celestial bodies appear along its length.

Crusading (Rare). The Cleric’s spellcasting skills help the characters defeat a group of fiendish cultists. The DM decides the wand evolves to become Rare, gaining the Crusading property.

Lunar (Very Rare). The characters track down a devil that serves the Fiend the cultists worshipped. Thanks to the Cleric, the characters defeat the devil, and the DM decides the wand evolves, becoming Very Rare and gaining the Lunar property.

Heliacal (Legendary). The Cleric becomes a paragon of his deity, so the DM decides the wand evolves to channel the might of a supernova, becoming Legendary and gaining the Heliacal property.

Evolving Magic Items.name: Evolving Magic Items
Evolving Magic Items.text:
Few experiences infuse players with more wonder than their characters finding exciting magic items. Characters often grow fond of magic items that have personal significance, such as items that remind them of a beloved companion or a heroic deed.

As characters grow in power, though, that fondness can turn to frustration. A level 1 character’s beloved Uncommon item might no longer be as useful by the time that character reaches level 5. Eventually, the character might have a dilemma: abandon their favorite magic item in favor of one with less personal significance, or keep the favored item, potentially forgoing a mechanically stronger option.

The magic item evolution rules in this section allow you to grant a magic item additional properties and increase its rarity as characters become more powerful. With these tools, you can build narrative significance into your characters’ magic items and enable the items to grow in power as the characters do. This section presents several ready-made evolving magic items and rules for evolving certain magic items from the Dungeon Master’s Guide or other sources.

Custom Evolving Magic Items.name: Custom Evolving Magic Items
Custom Evolving Magic Items.text:
You can use magic items from the Dungeon Master’s Guide as the basis for evolving magic items.

This section presents two methods for creating your own evolving magic items: simple evolution and complex evolution.

Simple Evolution

Complex Evolution

Some magic items can grow in strength beyond increasing the bonuses they grant. By granting a magic item new and more powerful magical properties, you can create an evolving magic item that grows in exciting ways.

Using the rules in this section, you can evolve eligible magic items from the Dungeon Master’s Guide. At your discretion, items from other sources might be eligible for evolution using these rules.

The following magic items are eligible for complex evolution:

Certain Rods and Wands: Any Rod of the Pact Keeper or Wand of the War Mage

Certain Other Uncommon or Rarer Magic Items: Any Armor, Staff, or Weapon that requires Attunement, that isn’t cursed, and whose rarity is at most Very Rare

Complex Evolution Steps. To evolve an item with this system, use the following steps in conjunction with the instructions from “When to Evolve Magic Items” earlier in this chapter:

1: Choose a Magic Item to Evolve. Pick the eligible magic item you plan to evolve, and note its current rarity.

2: Determine the Item’s New Rarity. The item’s new rarity is the next highest rarity.

3: Roll on or Choose from the New Rarity’s Table. Use the Magic Item Properties table for the item’s new rarity to select a new property, noting any details such as limited usage. (If the magic item grants a bonus to Armor Class, attack and damage rolls, saving throws, or spell save DCs, don’t increase the bonus as part of evolving the item with this system. For example, if you evolve a +1 Wand of the War Mage and give it a new property from this system, the item’s bonus remains +1.)

4: Determine the Item’s New Name and Physical Characteristics. Change the evolved item’s name to represent its newfound power. If you like, you can give the item a new, more dramatic name. Either way, preface its name with the name of the property it just gained. For example, if you evolve a Sword of Sharpness to be Legendary and grant it the Prismatic property, it would be called a Prismatic Sword of Sharpness. Evolution also causes physical changes; examples include the appearance of magical runes or additional filigree.

Magical Specializations.name: Magical Specializations
Magical Specializations.text:
With the exception of the Ninth Quill, each of these magical factions specializes in a particular school of magic, as shown in the Factions by School table. Ninth Quill members instead dabble in all disciplines. These specializations are as much philosophical as technical. For instance, the fireball-throwing evokers of the Crucible Keepers are often forceful personalities who enjoy dramatic displays of destructive magic. In contrast, the subtle enchanters of the Bejeweled Conclave prefer to use smooth words to achieve their goals.

Magical factions include spellcasters who specialize in the associated school of magic. A faction’s base of operations counts as a city for the purpose of purchasing spellcasting services (described in the Player’s Handbook) for spells of the associated school. At your discretion, the casting of spells that belong to other schools might also be available for purchase, and faction members might offer discounts based on the characters’ relationship with the faction.

Renown.text: Characters can undertake missions and do favors for a faction and thereby earn renown with that faction without necessarily becoming members of the organization. Each faction description in this chapter includes benefits characters gain from accruing renown with the faction (as detailed in the Dungeon Master’s Guide).

Joining Factions.name: Joining Factions
Joining Factions.text:
Although most members of magical factions are spellcasters, characters of any class can find a home in one or more of these factions. Each description includes the process for becoming a member of the faction; the benefits for doing so; and recommendations for classes, backgrounds, and proficiencies that make characters particularly well suited to the faction. The Factions by Class table provides a summary of which factions are a good fit for each class from the Player’s Handbook.

Special Facilities

Each faction detailed in this chapter includes a special facility that members of that faction can add to their Bastions. The rules for Bastions appear in the Dungeon Master’s Guide.

Faction Descriptions.name: Faction Descriptions
Faction Descriptions.text:
This chapter includes details on the following factions:

Bejeweled Conclave. The discreet enchanters of the Bejeweled Conclave make themselves invaluable to powerful clients as elite entertainers, advisers, and mediators while amassing clients’ secrets.

Bringers of Cosmic Dawn. Reclusive transmuters obsessed with mutations, the Bringers of Cosmic Dawn seek guidance from alien intelligences.

Covenant of the Grave. The necromancers of the Covenant of the Grave study death and undeath with scientific precision, seeking esoteric knowledge through rigorous research.

Crucible Keepers. From volcanic eruptions to shore-shredding hurricanes, no natural disaster is too dangerous for the daring Crucible Keepers to study in their pursuit of ever-escalating applications for Evocation magic.

Horizon Weavers. The Horizon Weavers’ conjurers practice summoning and teleportation as they explore and chart the multiverse.

Ninth Quill. The spies and saboteurs of the Ninth Quill steal lore and artifacts from other powerful mages; many members do so to safeguard these treasures, but others are motivated by greed. The Ninth Quill also stokes dissent among the other factions to keep them from growing too powerful.

Phantasmic Circus. The showy illusionists of the Phantasmic Circus entertain eager audiences with impossible spectacles.

Seers of Sea and Sky. The diligent oracles of the Seers of Sea and Sky divine truths in the movements of the wind and waves.

Sheltering Hands. The abjurers of the Sheltering Hands uplift the downtrodden and protect those in need.

Groundlings.name: Groundlings
Groundlings.text:
Skulking Hybrid Servitors

Habitat: Hill, Urban; Treasure: Armaments

Groundlings are hairy, stinky bullies and insatiable carnivores. They use their claws not only to disembowel their victims but also to dig traps, tunnel beneath buildings, and excavate hiding spots from which to ambush prey.

Groundlings are created, not born. Most are magical mutations of fierce burrowing animals. Groundlings often serve as shock troops or assassins for their creators, though leaderless groundlings sometimes pursue lives as killers or mercenaries.

Groundlings are victims of heinous magic. The brutality of evil never ends, and thus we must continue to fight against it.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.book.JournalEntry.aunArtHandoutsG2.JournalEntryPage.DlHezTTWfTUWDYGZ classes="overlay-caption" cite=false]

Groundling Grunt.name: Groundling Grunt
Groundling Grunt.text:
Created to be brute troops, groundling grunts love tearing flesh with their claws. If not controlled by a commanding leader, they’re likely to slip away and pursue mayhem or to stop during a battle to feast on their kills.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.actors.Actor.aunGroundlingGru caption=false cite=true statblock classes="double-column hide-in-embed"]

Groundling Stalker.name: Groundling Stalker
Groundling Stalker.text:
Groundling stalkers enjoy ambushing and murdering foes from afar with their crossbows. Stalkers rarely maintain the element of surprise for long, as they roar in bloodthirsty delight when they strike.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.actors.Actor.aunGroundlingSta caption=false cite=true statblock classes="double-column hide-in-embed"]

Groundling Slayer.name: Groundling Slayer
Groundling Slayer.text:
A groundling that learns subtlety and self-control becomes an efficient killer. These groundling slayers are often entrusted with solo missions of stealth or assassination or are assigned to keep fractious groundlings in line. Slayers usually wait until after a fight is over before consuming foes they’ve slain.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.actors.Actor.aunGroundlingSla caption=false cite=true statblock classes="double-column hide-in-embed"]

Horizon Weavers.name: Horizon Weavers
Horizon Weavers.text:
The Horizon Weavers is a collection of far-flung conjurers, explorers, and scholars who practice summoning, teleportation, and planar travel.

Members of the Horizon Weavers have unparalleled wanderlust; they’ve seen sights and lived through experiences most would consider too wild to be true. However, the faction’s planar sojourns have not gone unnoticed, and members now work to avert the attention of a malevolent extraplanar entity fixated on their organization.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.book.JournalEntry.aunArtHandoutsG2.JournalEntryPage.6XMqMUMy4tmYxs9E classes=overlay-caption cite=false]

Goals and Activities.name: Goals and Activities
Goals and Activities.text:
Horizon Weavers hone their expertise in all forms of Conjuration magic, from summoning to creation to teleportation, with a focus on extraplanar travel. Powerful Horizon Weavers create gates between planes, while junior members catalog known gates or simply wander through to see what’s on the other side. New faction members usually begin by traveling their own world to experience different climates and cultures before exploring other planes.

Many faction members are also amateur or professional artisans; some weave textiles as well as magic. Horizon Weavers often incorporate spells such as @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.spells.Item.phbsplFindFamili]{Find Familiar} or @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.spells.Item.phbsplMageHand00]{Mage Hand} into their everyday lives, using magic for everything from companionship to household chores.

Horizon Weaver Cloaks

Each new member who joins the faction receives a durable cloak with their initials sewn into the collar. Horizon Weavers recognize these garments on sight and seek to retrieve any that are lost or stolen.

A Horizon Weaver’s cloak repels water and protects its wearer from most types of weather. The faction replaces damaged cloaks when necessary. Some members weave the threads of former cloaks into new ones.

Many Horizon Weavers incorporate their cloaks into magic items they create. The most popular choices are @UUID[Compendium.dnd-dungeon-masters-guide.equipment.Item.dmgCapeOfTheMoun]{Cape of the Mountebank}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-dungeon-masters-guide.equipment.Item.dmgCloakOfProtec]{Cloak of Protection}, and @UUID[Compendium.dnd-dungeon-masters-guide.equipment.Item.dmgClothesOfMend]{Clothes of Mending}.

The Lurker

A massive beast from the liminal space between planes menaces the Horizon Weavers. This entity, known as the Lurker, towers higher than mountains, with immense pincers and a single, enormous eye that radiates malice and reflects strange lights and lines.

Several months ago, when faction members first glimpsed the Lurker, a powerful team of Horizon Weavers set out to confront the monster. The team went missing, and the Lurker has since become more aggressive, snapping at some Horizon Weavers in the split second it takes them to magically travel between planes. Sometimes this shears the unlucky traveler in half; other times, the individual never reappears. These incidents are rare, but all Horizon Weavers worry about a potential Lurker strike with each planar trip.

Those who provide shelter and aid to explorers of this vast multiverse are friends to both me and Mystra.

Leadership and Organization.name: Leadership and Organization
Leadership and Organization.text:
As befits members of a society of explorers, Horizon Weavers are widely scattered. A wandering Horizon Weaver might go weeks or months without seeing another member, and a meeting might be coincidental. Senior faction members, called Gatemakers, settle disputes or provide advice, although reaching a Gatemaker often requires a cross-planar trek.

Way Stations and Shuttles

Not all Horizon Weavers seek endless travel. Some stay in one place for months or years, perhaps with a friend or lover they met during their travels. Horizon Weavers who remain in one place are expected to maintain way stations, providing directions, supplies, and shelter to passing faction members.

Weaving slang is common in these way stations: a “shuttle” is a traveler, a “beam” is a well-established way station, a “weft” is a member with irrepressible wanderlust, and a “heddle” is someone reliable.

You can roll on the Planar Way Stations table to generate a sample way station or odd planar locale.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.tables.RollTable.aunPlanarWaySt1D rollable resultLabel="Location" captionPosition=top]{Planar Way Stations}

Joining the Horizon Weavers

Any curious adventurer who longs to explore the unknown might join the faction after meeting a Horizon Weaver. An extended conversation with a member is all it takes to earn a second meeting, when the member presents the aspirant with a Horizon Weaver cloak and officially inducts them into the organization. An inducting member without weaving skills or connections might invite the new member to create their own Horizon Weaver cloak, though it must be made to the faction’s specifications.

Spiral Conservatory

Deep in a forest on the Material Plane stands a twisting building of wood and stone that surrounds a grassy courtyard. This is the Spiral Conservatory, the first and largest Horizon Weaver way station. Here, students of Conjuration magic and planar lore learn to navigate hazardous environments, summon helpful creatures, and conjure useful equipment.

The Spiral Conservatory is located at a confluence of ley lines that provides numerous, if inconstant, gates to Arcadia, the Beastlands, and the Feywild. Fey and intelligent animals often wander through the Spiral Conservatory; some of them delight in mentoring eager Horizon Weavers.

A tiefling named Gallinaver the Heddle (Medium @UUID[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.actors.Actor.aunConjurerArchm]{Conjurer Archmage}; see chapter 6) serves as the Spiral Conservatory’s chief caretaker. Gallinaver and his husband, a soft-spoken @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmDjinni00000000]{Djinni} named Cloud Lace, are the easiest Gatemakers to contact, as they’re never far from the Spiral Conservatory.

Renown Rewards.name: Renown Rewards
Renown Rewards.text:
Characters gain renown with the Horizon Weavers by displaying planar knowledge, conjuring magical wonders, reporting previously unknown planar gates, or completing excursions for the faction. As their Renown Scores increase, characters gain access to various perks, as shown on the Horizon Weavers Renown table. If your campaign doesn’t use renown, the DM decides if and when characters earn these perks.

Horizon Weavers Renown

Renown Score

Reward

3+

You can consult with the Horizon Weavers to receive general information about a plane you intend to visit.

5+

You can stay in any way station maintained by a Horizon Weaver (including the Spiral Conservatory).

The first time your Renown Score reaches 10, the faction gives you an Uncommon magic item from the Armor or Wondrous Item category. Alternatively, if you’re a member, the faction can craft your faction cloak into an Uncommon magic item of your choice.

You receive a 10 percent discount when buying armor, weapons, and adventuring gear from a Horizon Weaver way station.

You are given one of a pair of Sending Stones ; the other is held by a mid-level faction member. If you are lost in an extraplanar location the faction can reach, you can use the Sending Stone to call the faction for help. [[/r 1d4]] @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmScoutCaptain00]{Scout Captains} then arrive to escort you to a safe destination. If your Renown Score drops below 20, your @UUID[Compendium.dnd-dungeon-masters-guide.equipment.Item.dmgSendingStones]{Sending Stone} is confiscated.

The discount you receive at way stations increases to 20 percent.

The first time your Renown Score reaches 30, the faction teaches you to traverse liminal spaces. You always have the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.spells.Item.phbsplMistyStep0]{Misty Step} spell prepared, and you can cast it once without expending a spell slot. You regain the ability to cast it in this way when you finish a Long Rest. Intelligence, Wisdom, or Charisma is your spellcasting ability for this spell (choose when you gain this reward). You can also cast this spell using any spell slots you have of the appropriate level.

40+

You can arrange for a meeting with any of the faction’s Gatemakers. Once you use this reward, you can’t do so again until your Renown Score increases.

50+

Faction members can cast the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.spells.Item.phbsplPlaneShift]{Plane Shift} spell at your behest, transporting you and your allies to an extraplanar location of your choice. Once you use this reward, you can’t do so again until your Renown Score increases.

Horizon Weavers Characters.name: Horizon Weavers Characters
Horizon Weavers Characters.text:
The Horizon Weavers welcome carefree, capable wanderers who yearn to see what’s over the horizon or through a planar portal.

@UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.classes.Item.phbdrdDruid00000]{Druids}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.classes.Item.phbrgrRanger0000]{Rangers}, and @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.classes.Item.phbwzdWizard0000]{Wizards} (especially those with the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.subclasses.Item.aunConjurer00000]{Conjurer} subclass; see chapter 1) are excellent fits. Characters with proficiency in Arcana or Survival; proficiency with Navigator’s Tools or Weaver’s Tools; or the @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.origins.Item.phbbgArtisan0000]{Artisan}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.origins.Item.phbbgGuide000000]{Guide}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.backgrounds.Item.aunHorizonWeavmB]{Horizon Weaver Initiate} (see chapter 1), or @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.origins.Item.phbbgWayfarer000]{Wayfarer} background are also welcome.

Member Benefits

If you’re a member of the Horizon Weavers, you receive these benefits.

Traveling Cloak. You receive a distinctive Horizon Weavers cloak and a set of @UUID[Compendium.dnd-players-handbook.equipment.Item.phbagClothesTrav]{Traveler’s Clothes}.

Trinket. Roll on the Horizon Weavers Trinkets table to determine what trinket you have from your time with the Horizon Weavers.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.tables.RollTable.aunHorizonWeavlu rollable resultLabel="Trinket" captionPosition=top]{Horizon Weavers Trinkets}

Using This Faction.name: Using This Faction
Using This Faction.text:
The Horizon Weavers might give out quests, such as mapmaking or rescue missions, that require travel to distant places. They might also seek the adventurers’ help dealing with the threat of the Lurker.

The Horizon Weavers can also rescue characters stranded in distant or inhospitable places, such as those sent to other planes by the Prismatic Spray or Prismatic Wall spell. Lost characters might be lucky enough to find a Horizon Weaver way station.

Special Facility.name: Special Facility
Special Facility.text:
Members of the Horizon Weavers can add the following special facility to their Bastions.

@UUID[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.bastions.Item.aunPlanarGateway]{Planar Gateway}

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.bastions.Item.aunPlanarGateway caption=false cite=false]

Living Spells.name: Living Spells
Living Spells.text:
Animate Magical Effects

Habitat: Any; Treasure: None

Magical energies unleashed during cataclysmic battles or catastrophic experiments can cause spell effects to come to life as living spells. These beings’ magical energy is persistent, and they bear features resembling those of their origin spells—usually Conjuration or Evocation spells. Living spells typically linger in the region of their creation, subsisting on ambient magical energy and lashing out at creatures they encounter.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.book.JournalEntry.aunArtHandoutsG2.JournalEntryPage.UanoQsZ0yRDnyeFa classes="overlay-caption" cite=false]

Creating Living Spells.name: Creating Living Spells
Creating Living Spells.text:
Living spells come in many varieties; the stat blocks here are three examples. To make a living spell from a different spell, choose a damage-dealing Conjuration or Evocation spell of level 1–5 from the Wizard spell list. Then consult the Living Spell Customization table to see which stat block to customize based on the chosen spell’s level.

Living Spell Customization

Spell Level

Stat Block to Customize

1–2

Living Thunderwave

3–4

Living Vitriolic Sphere

5

Living Cone of Cold

Now make the following changes to the stat block:

Damage Immunity. Replace the living spell’s damage Immunity with Immunity to the type (or types) of damage dealt by the chosen spell.

Magical Strike. Change the damage type dealt by Magical Strike to one of the damage types dealt by the chosen spell.

Spell Mimicry. Replace the effect of Spell Mimicry with the effect of the chosen spell. If that spell requires a saving throw, use the spell save DC from Spell Mimicry. If the spell involves an attack roll, use the attack bonus from the living spell’s Magical Strike.

For example, if you turn Fireball (a level 3 spell) into a living spell, customize the Living Vitriolic Sphere stat block. The living fireball has Immunity to Fire damage instead of Acid damage, deals Fire damage with its Magical Strike, and replicates Fireball with Spell Mimicry.

Living Thunderwave.name: Living Thunderwave
Living Thunderwave.text:
A living thunderwave roars and rumbles, booming with thunder like an unnatural storm cloud.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.actors.Actor.aunLivingThunder caption=false cite=true statblock classes="double-column hide-in-embed"]

Living Vitriolic Sphere.name: Living Vitriolic Sphere
Living Vitriolic Sphere.text:
A living vitriolic sphere is a perpetually roiling, fuming miasma. It scars the ground beneath itself with dribbles of acid.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.actors.Actor.aunLivingVitriol caption=false cite=true statblock classes="double-column hide-in-embed"]

Living Cone of Cold.name: Living Cone of Cold
Living Cone of Cold.text:
Accompanied by blasts of frigid wind, a living cone of cold seeks sources of heat—such as living creatures—to freeze solid.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.actors.Actor.aunLivingConeOfC caption=false cite=true statblock classes="double-column hide-in-embed"]

Magical Factions.name: Magical Factions
Magical Factions.text:
Many scholars and practitioners of magic seek ever-greater prowess and status, but few can achieve these individually. Instead, those pursuing mystical knowledge often join influential groups. Numerous in membership and great in achievement, these factions accept adventurers into their folds, offering resources and knowledge in exchange for loyalty and service.

Each faction described in this chapter has its own outlook and goals, such as providing magical advice and entertainment to influence the powerful, researching alien forces from beyond the stars, and uncovering the secrets of life and undeath.

Faction members exchange magical discoveries, mentor pupils, and learn from more experienced colleagues. Members are united by shared specialties and philosophies. Although these organizations’ disparate objectives often bring them into conflict with each other, members of different factions might also unite over common goals.

You can use these factions as patrons, as villains, or as organizations the characters can join. Adapt them to your world or campaign as needed.

How Patrons Work.name: How Patrons Work
How Patrons Work.text:
No matter their details, group patrons provide adventurers with some common benefits.

Group Assistance

Having a group patron gives an adventuring group a common purpose, which inspires better coordination in the form of guidance and encouragement. As a result of this connection, each member of your party can grant Advantage on a D20 Test made by another member of the party. To grant Advantage in this way, you and your target must be able to see or hear each other, and neither can have the Incapacitated condition. After granting Advantage in this way, you can’t do so again until you finish a Long Rest.

Perks

Group patrons offer characters perks ranging from a steady wage to access to libraries and magical resources to unexpected allies. Specific perks are presented in the description of each group patron.

Option: Make Your Patron Mysterious.name: Option: Make Your Patron Mysterious
Option: Make Your Patron Mysterious.text:
@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.book.JournalEntry.aunArtHandoutsG2.JournalEntryPage.5UdeCi1PrQ0SsuOR classes=overlay-caption cite=false]

Concealing the true identity of your group patron can be a fun campaign linchpin, especially if your game involves magic-themed intrigue. Any of the magical group patrons described in this chapter might have reasons to stay anonymous. If you use a mysterious patron, create a strong reason the patron is hiding their identity.

High-Profile Patron

A group patron might remain anonymous because they’re incredibly powerful, famous or infamous, or otherwise high profile, and their identity being known would undermine the characters’ goals or ability to operate clandestinely. Or the patron might have reasons they wish to remain publicly unassociated with the characters. For example, perhaps the patron is a powerful political figure who can’t publicly take sides in a civil dispute but wants the characters to side with freedom fighters over greedy merchants.

Ulterior Motives

On the other hand, a patron might hide their identity because their motives are malevolent. The patron might try to trick the characters into performing deeds that destabilize a fragile peace or empower an evil overlord. Or a patron might remain anonymous because the characters would never knowingly work for them, especially if the patron is nefarious and the heroes are upstanding.

Kindness promotes peace and good, but the practicalities of the world require coin. A patron who supplies the latter is useful; a patron who also believes in you is invaluable.

Concealing Their Identity

Mysterious magical patrons don’t show their true faces to the characters, communicating via anonymous letters, prearranged signals, and networks of underlings similarly unaware of the patron’s identity. A mysterious patron might refer to themself with a code name that fits the nature of the missions they ask the characters to undertake. In this case, the characters can’t gain benefits associated with the patron’s identity, such as the archmage’s and esoteric institution’s Documentation perks or the magical entity’s Name Drop perk. Instead, the characters must find ways other than invoking their patron’s name to achieve their goals.

Using Magic. Since magical patrons are typically powerful mages, they use high-level spell effects to ensure the characters don’t discover their identity. A patron might repeatedly use the Programmed Illusion spell to convey information to the characters via fictional, illusory agents. If a patron must interact with a character, the patron might use the Seeming spell to significantly alter their appearance. Similarly, a patron might use the Mirage Arcane spell to conceal their lair’s true location behind an illusory waterfall or trees. As your characters gain power, ensure their patron uses magic that the characters are unlikely to dispel.

Keeping the Characters on Board. If you use a mysterious group patron in your game, it’s important for the characters to remain convinced that the patron’s goals align with theirs. Attribute to the patron’s code name deeds that are benevolent or helpful to the characters. Or ensure the patron compensates the characters well for their work, giving the characters a practical reason to continue working for them.

The Big Reveal

Eventually, the novelty of being sponsored by a mysterious group patron will wear thin. The characters might lose interest in working for someone unwilling to reveal their identity. They might begin to distrust or become frustrated with the patron.

When the time is right, you might reveal the patron’s identity. You can do so suddenly, with the patron meeting the characters in person to thank them for their work, or more subtly.

Dropping Hints. As the characters complete more of the patron’s missions, the patron might begin to drop—intentionally or unintentionally—coded hints about their identity. Investigating these clues can become a fun side quest for the characters.

Benevolent Patron. Once the characters have solved the clues, the patron might appear in person to congratulate them on discovering the secret. The patron might have intended to reveal themself once the characters proved themselves worthy through solving the clues, or the characters might have preempted the patron’s plans. Either way, this gradual approach provides satisfaction to characters eager to learn their patron’s identity.

Malevolent Patron. If the patron’s motives are malicious, the characters might react with horror to their patron’s identity. In this case, providing a satisfying conclusion to your campaign involves the characters confirming their patron’s identity and formulating a plan for dealing with them. That might involve leaving the patron’s employ abruptly, turning the tables on the patron to discredit them, confronting the patron in combat, or another option.

Follow your players’ lead in how to wrap up the campaign. You might decide that the patron anticipated the characters’ realization, but keep in mind that defeating this duplicitous patron allows a satisfying conclusion.

Archmage.name: Archmage
Archmage.text:
As incredibly powerful spellcasters, archmages are capable of impressive deeds. Beyond slaying dragons or destroying undead, archmages have saved (and ruled!) entire cities, driven back armies, defeated the forces of the Nine Hells or the Abyss, and traveled in time. The mightiest archmages achieve magical mastery over the physical world. Some no longer age, spending centuries amassing unfathomable magical knowledge and prowess and creating spells they name after themselves.

With archmages’ great learning and magical capabilities comes even greater willpower. Standing among the multiverse’s strongest personalities, archmages personify stubbornness (even among the best) and self-centeredness (prominent among the worst). This unyielding nature translates into a voracious drive, whether it’s to protect the weak, combat the wicked, amass the most knowledge, or take the biggest risks.

Archmage Motivations

Archmages might patronize a group for the following reasons:

Emissaries Are Needed. Archmages amass allies and commune with powerful leaders during their travels throughout the multiverse. An archmage hires the characters to travel to these allies and request their aid—or aid those allies—in the archmage’s pursuit of friendly relations or magical research.

Evil Is Rising. Benevolent archmages recognize the sheer power of unchecked evil and are sensitive to such forces amassing strength or plotting terrible deeds. An archmage who discovers complex and wicked schemes hires the characters to complete tasks that undermine those schemes.

Lieutenants Are Required. An archmage who identifies numerous threats plaguing a certain area hires the characters to face a host of lesser threats so the archmage can focus on powerful villainous leaders.

Archmage Patrons

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.book.JournalEntry.aunArtHandoutsG2.JournalEntryPage.MvdyGRl7NAJbc8Zl classes="float-right overlay-caption" cite=false]

The following characters from the D&D multiverse could serve as archmage group patrons:

Alustriel Silverhand. One of the most powerful mages in the Forgotten Realms setting, Alustriel has been a proponent of good and enemy of evil for centuries. Alustriel is an immortal human daughter of Mystra, a god of magic, and ruled the city of Silverymoon for centuries. Alustriel maintains safe houses scattered across the planes for her allies as they promote compassion throughout the multiverse.

Vajra Safahr. Chief mage of Waterdeep in the Forgotten Realms setting, the human Vajra is the youngest head in the history of Blackstaff Academy, a school for mages. While Vajra fends off threats to her city and her university, she also faces political conflicts from those who would unseat her from her place of prestige.

Yolande. Known as the Faerie Queen, Yolande is the benevolent and beloved elf monarch of the nation of Celene in the world of Greyhawk. She is a mighty wizard who protects her nation against the incursion of Elemental Evil forces as well as threats against the Feywild and the Material Plane.

Creating Your Own Archmage

Instead of using one of the archmages described above, you can create an archmage to serve as a group patron for your characters. You might start by choosing one of the eight archmage stat blocks in chapter 6, each of which specializes in one school of magic, and add personality details as you see fit.

When creating an archmage, consider how close to the traditional archetype you want your archmage to be. A traditional archmage is incredibly powerful and eccentric. They’re easily distracted because they’re nurturing layers of complicated schemes. Your archmage could be very different: plain spoken, attentive to the characters, not as powerful as their reputation would suggest—or far more so.

When you create an archmage for your campaign, you can roll on or choose from the Archmage Type table to determine details of the archmage’s persona.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.tables.RollTable.aunArchmageTyp9A rollable resultLabel="Patron Type" captionPosition=top]{Archmage Type}

Archmage Patron Perks

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.book.JournalEntry.aunArtHandoutsG2.JournalEntryPage.hFPMUSJhhpvUX9mK classes="float-right overlay-caption" cite=false]

Characters in a party whose patron is an archmage gain the following perks.

Compensation. Archmages amass considerable wealth during their adventures and travels, and archmage patrons generously compensate their underlings. The nature of your work for an archmage influences how you’re paid. On average, the archmage pays each member of your group 2 GP per day (enough to sustain a Comfortable lifestyle). Or you might be paid (at least 300 GP) each time you complete a task the archmage assigns.

Documentation. Each member of your group has identification noting their affiliation with the archmage, which carries clout in areas where the archmage is known. If the archmage is the ruler of a city or nation, the documentation grants the characters appropriate authority in that realm.

Magical Resources. Archmages collect untold magic items and magical curiosities, though these collections are often scattered among far-flung sanctums. An archmage can give you any Common or Uncommon magic item in the Dungeon Master’s Guide, as long as possession of the item would help your group’s tasks. When your group reaches level 11, the archmage can retrieve one Rare and one Very Rare magic item in between the group’s tasks and award it to you as additional compensation. When your group reaches level 17, the archmage can retrieve one Rare, Very Rare, or Legendary magic item in between tasks and award it to you as additional compensation.

Spellcasting. Archmages can use their spellpower to help your missions. An archmage can cast any level 1 or lower spell for you at no cost, as long as the spell’s effects would aid your work. The archmage can cast any level 2–8 spell for you at half the usual cost.

Archmage Contacts

An archmage group patron might prioritize working with the characters, meeting with the party directly to deliver missions and collect reports. In this case, the archmage becomes a significant recurring character in your campaign, so give the archmage a manner of speaking or another feature that makes them distinctive. For example, the archmage might talk to their snake familiar, wear outrageously garish outfits, or hum odd tunes when distracted.

But archmages have a lot to do, and the patron might send a representative in their place. Roll on or choose from the Archmage Contact table to determine how the archmage interacts with the characters.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.tables.RollTable.aunArchmageConPu rollable resultLabel="Contact Type" captionPosition=top]{Archmage Contact}

An Archmage Campaign

A campaign driven by an archmage patron might unfold according to this outline:

Levels 1–4. As the characters begin their adventuring career, the archmage watches them from afar, monitoring their activities and subtly directing their attention to the groundlings (see chapter 6) that a wicked rival archmage commands.

Levels 5–10. The archmage reveals themself to the characters and hires the characters to investigate the rival archmage, whose schemes threaten the city or surrounding realm. You can use the stat block for one of the archmages in chapter 6 for this rival, whom the party confronts in a climactic battle.

Levels 11–16. The archmage patron sends the characters all over the world to gather magical secrets from creatures that hoard knowledge; adult dragons, devils, and a @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmDemilich000000]{Demilich} make suitable antagonists.

Levels 17–20. The archmage patron retires. The characters are now obliged to deal with the archmage’s enemies and rivals while exploring the archmage’s extraplanar lair.

Esoteric Institution.name: Esoteric Institution
Esoteric Institution.text:
An esoteric institution might be a magical academy, an order of monks researching lost magical techniques, or any other organization focused on the study, preservation, and use of magical lore. Institutions usually maintain a base of operations such as a campus, monastery, or remote fortress. The institution might have a large staff including administrators, teachers, groundskeepers, and guards. In addition to an excellent library, it probably has a secure vault for storing dangerous magic items, and more than one Artifact might be housed there.

Esoteric institutions have a long history that stretches back generations. In that time, an institution has made enemies and collected magic items that have been stored away and forgotten. The institution’s headquarters might have secret chambers protected by puzzles and traps. Despite its reclusive or insular nature, the institution monitors the world beyond its walls. When it finds magic being used for evil or learns of long-forgotten lore to be recovered, it sends adventurers on missions.

Esoteric Institution Motivations

An esoteric institution might patronize a group for the following reasons:

The Characters Are Students. The characters are students at an academy such as the Tower of High Sorcery in the Dragonlance setting or Strixhaven University and are sent on missions as part of their studies. The institution doesn’t intentionally send the characters on dangerous missions, and it sends rescue teams if the characters get into trouble while pursuing goals tied to the academy.

The Institution Needs Field Agents. An esoteric institution includes sages, scholars, and researchers, but few warriors and explorers. The institution wants to hire the characters for missions deemed too dangerous for its own staff, such as rescuing students in peril.

The Characters Are Specialists. An esoteric institution seeks out the characters because the characters are experts in a particular field relevant to a current problem or interest. For example, if the characters recently defeated a powerful vampire, the institution hires them to recover that vampire’s hidden library of magical tomes.

Esoteric Institution Patrons

The following organizations from the D&D multiverse could serve as esoteric institution group patrons:

Order of the Guardians. The Order of the Guardians is a group of ascetics who gather, sequester, and protect dangerous magic in the Ravenloft setting. Its members maintain several hidden and well-protected monasteries, but the largest is Watchers’ Stronghold in the Mistlands, a piece of the disintegrating domain of Darkon. The order is stretched thin, outnumbered and outmatched by the horrors found in the Domains of Dread, and it’s quick to hire adventurers willing to venture into dangerous sites to recover powerful items or spells so they can’t be used for evil. More information on the Order of the Guardians and Darkon can be found in Ravenloft: The Horrors Within.

Thebestys. In the Outlands of the Planescape setting, the walled city of Thebestys is home to an ibis-headed, many-named god of learning. This god maintains a great library at the city’s center. The library enjoys a reputation as a matchless repository of knowledge. The ibis-headed god employs the characters as agents who travel through the city of Sigil and the planes to find books and bring them back to the library for copying and collection. Thebestys and the Outlands are detailed in Planescape: Adventures in the Multiverse.

Tower of High Sorcery. In the Dragonlance setting, there were once five Towers of High Sorcery, where mages were trained. Due to disaster and tragedy, only one remains. There, spellcasters study magic in traditions tied to the world of Krynn’s three moons. Characters in this setting serve the mages of the tower as teachers, students, or defenders, and they are dispatched to locations across the world to preserve magical secrets from the destructive draconian army. You can find more information on the Tower of High Sorcery in Dragonlance: Shadow of the Dragon Queen.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.book.JournalEntry.aunArtHandoutsG2.JournalEntryPage.w521xER8rWjU4wBQ classes=overlay-caption cite=false]

Creating Your Own Esoteric Institution

Instead of using one of the esoteric institutions described above, you can create an institution to serve as a group patron for your characters. This gives you an opportunity to customize the institution to appeal to your players and to reflect the characters they’ve created. For example, if your players have made wilderness-oriented characters such as Barbarians, Druids, and Rangers, the institution you create is likely focused on preserving nature. If you want tension between the characters and the institution, the leaders of the institution might be of different alignments than the characters.

When you create an esoteric institution for your campaign, roll on or choose from the Esoteric Institution Type table to inspire the institution’s details.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.tables.RollTable.aunEsotericInszl rollable resultLabel="Contact Type" captionPosition=top]{Esoteric Institution Type}

Esoteric Institution Patron Perks

Characters in a party whose patron is an esoteric institution gain the following perks.

Compensation. The institution pays for the work you do on its behalf. The nature of your employment influences your compensation. On average, the institution pays each member of your group 1 GP per day (or enough to sustain a Modest lifestyle). Or you might be paid a bounty (at least 250 GP) for each magic item or piece of lore you bring back from your adventures and give to the institution.

Documentation. Each member of your group has identification noting their affiliation with the institution, which carries clout in areas where the institution is known. For magical academies such as the Tower of High Sorcery or Strixhaven, this is a letter on official stationery marked with the academy’s seal, but for secretive organizations like the Order of the Guardians, the documentation takes the form of a signet ring or brooch marked with a discreet symbol.

Esoteric Research. Esoteric institutions include expansive libraries specializing in magical knowledge. When you take a Bastion turn, you can (as a group) issue the Research order to the institution as if it were a Library facility in your Bastion. The topic chosen must be related to magic in some way; at the DM’s discretion, the institution can research topics related to the planes as well. Once you reach level 13, you instead can issue the Research order to the institution as if it were an Archive.

Scroll and Spellbook Access. You have access to the institution’s library of Spell Scrolls and spellbooks, as well as supplies for copying spells. You can buy any Spell Scroll from the institution for half its usual value, as indicated in the Dungeon Master’s Guide. You can find any spell from the Player’s Handbook in the library, and the institution pays half the GP cost of copying the spell.

Training. You have access to continuing education at no cost. You can spend 30 days in classes to gain one of the following benefits of your choice:

Skill. You gain proficiency in one of these skills of your choice: Arcana, History, Nature, or Religion. You can gain proficiency in only one skill in this way.

Tool. You gain proficiency with a tool of your choice.

Language. You learn a language of your choice.

Esoteric Institution Contacts

An esoteric institution is typically large enough that the characters don’t know everyone in it, and its leaders are too busy to interact with the characters directly. Usually, one individual is the party’s contact, passing on instructions from the institution.

Think carefully about the contact’s personality, because your players will interact with them often. The contact doesn’t have to stay the same throughout the campaign; the institution might assign a new contact every mission or only in extreme circumstances.

Roll on or choose from the Esoteric Institution Contact table to determine who manages the relationship between the characters and the institution.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.tables.RollTable.aunEsotericInsbh rollable resultLabel="Contact Type" captionPosition=top]{Esoteric Institution Contact}

An Esoteric Institution Campaign

A campaign driven by an esoteric institution patron might unfold according to this outline:

Levels 1–4. The characters begin as students at an esoteric institution where they study magic. Their early adventures involve exploring the institution (overcoming animated objects and other guardians) and the surrounding region (perhaps populated by modrons, myconids, or undead). As part of their graduation exam, the characters are tasked to defeat a @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmBulette0000000]{Bulette} that threatens a nearby village.

Levels 5–10. Now graduates of the institution, the characters are sent on missions to dangerous, far-off places where magical lore is hidden or being used for evil. They battle cultists of an evil god of magic and infiltrate the lair of a young dragon or a nest of mind flayers.

Levels 11–16. Eventually the characters are offered senior positions at the institution, where they become teachers of a new generation of pupils. They must defend the institution against enemies such as @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmArcanaloth0000]{Arcanaloths}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmRakshasa000000]{Rakshasas}, and a @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmVampireUmbralL]{Vampire Umbral Lord}.

Levels 17–20. At the climax of the campaign, a traitorous member of the esoteric institution steals an item the party recovered earlier and tries to use it to attain vast power or simple vengeance. The traitor is being manipulated by a @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmPitFiend000000]{Pit Fiend}, and only the characters can stop them.

Magical Entity.name: Magical Entity
Magical Entity.text:
A magical entity is a powerful creature of mysterious or otherworldly origin. The entity might openly rule the realm in which they live, or they might be a mysterious figure that manipulates events from behind the scenes. Regardless, the magical entity is old, extremely knowledgeable, and frightening.

The magical entity is surrounded by legends and superstition. Villagers and townsfolk in the region know the entity by name. Most magical entities are feared as monsters, even if they’re benevolent, though some are revered as honorable creatures that protect the realm.

Magical Entity Motivations

Magical entities might patronize a group for the following reasons:

Bound to a Place. The magical entity is bound to a particular location and can’t leave. While supremely powerful and all but omniscient in their own realm, the being needs the characters to accomplish objectives beyond the entity’s reach.

Like Recognizes Like. The magical entity sees something in the characters that reminds the entity of themself. A good patron likely admires heroes who are kind and just, while an evil patron might be impressed by characters they perceive as proud and cruel.

Too Famous to Travel. The magical entity is so well known—and feared—that they can’t travel without attracting unwanted attention and alerting their enemies. The entity needs agents who can avoid notice.

Magical Entity Patrons

The following beings from the D&D multiverse could serve as magical entity patrons:

Baba Yaga. An arch-hag known as the Mother of All Witches, Baba Yaga travels the multiverse in her chicken-legged hut, pursuing inscrutable goals. She’s also the adoptive mother of the famous witch Tasha. Baba Yaga might hire characters of all alignments to seek esoteric magical knowledge or to act as her emissaries in formal political environments. Her goals and motivations are mysterious, but she offers great power to those she favors.

Bahamut. Bahamut is a god of good in numerous settings and is like a king to metallic dragons. He appears to mortals in various guises, often accompanied by seven yellow canaries that are gold dragons in disguise. In the world of Dragonlance, he has appeared as Fizban the Fabulous, a bumbling mage whose dramatic “accidents” often have hidden purposes. Bahamut is an excellent patron for good-aligned groups; he’s unlikely to work with evil characters unless he thinks they can be convinced to change their ways. He’s likely to conceal his true nature from the characters.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.book.JournalEntry.aunArtHandoutsG2.JournalEntryPage.vnDb6U5ABt9JrzFO classes=overlay-caption cite=false]

Strahd von Zarovich. Trapped in the domain of Barovia, the vampire Strahd is described in Ravenloft: The Horrors Within and Curse of Strahd. Strahd wields supreme power in his homeland, but he can’t leave it. He needs the characters to be his eyes and ears outside Barovia. Supremely egotistical, Strahd finds the idea of concealing his true identity entertaining for a while, but once the party has done a task or two for him, the mask comes off and the vampire reveals himself. Knowingly working with Strahd for an extended time likely won’t appeal to most heroic parties, though Strahd could make a great ongoing patron for amoral adventurers.

Creating Your Own Magical Entity

Instead of using one of the magical entities described above, you can create an entity to serve as a group patron for your characters. You might start by skimming through the Monster Manual looking for intelligent monsters with a CR of 13 or higher.

Even if your magical entity is frightening, strange, or otherworldly, that doesn’t mean the entity must be evil. Creatures commonly associated with evil deeds—such as chromatic dragons or undead—might have a change of heart and shift to a neutral or good alignment. But even a good magical entity can come across as weird, remote, or unsettling. Ordinary folk flee from the entity, but the characters are brave enough to interact with them.

When you create a magical entity for your campaign, you can roll on or choose from the Magical Entity Type table to determine the entity’s nature.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.tables.RollTable.aunMagicalEntiMs rollable resultLabel="Patron Type" captionPosition=top]{Magical Entity Type}

Magical Entity Patron Perks

Characters in a party whose patron is a magical entity gain the following perks.

Compensation. The magical entity pays for the work you do on their behalf. For every mission you successfully perform for the entity, you are rewarded with treasure worth 250 GP (or more, at the DM’s discretion). Your patron might reward you with Common or Uncommon magic items, especially consumables such as potions and Spell Scrolls.

Friends in Strange Places. Monsters of the same creature type as the magical entity are Friendly to you by default.

Name Drop. You can reveal the name of your group patron to your enemies, filling them with trepidation. When you make a Charisma (Intimidation) check to influence a creature, you can name your group patron, granting you Advantage on the check. If that check succeeds, you then gain a bonus to all checks made to influence that creature for 1 hour; the bonus is equal to half your level. Once you use this benefit, you can’t do so again until 7 days have passed.

Magical Entity Contacts

A magical entity is typically reclusive. Their unusual appearance and nature mean that they can’t simply walk down the streets of a settlement or meet the characters in a tavern—at least, not without an excellent disguise. For this reason, a magical entity is likely to communicate with the party through an intermediary or magical effect. But these contacts and effects, like the entity, should be unsettling or even scary.

Roll on or choose from the Magical Entity Contact table to determine how the magical entity interacts with the characters.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.tables.RollTable.aunMagicalEnti0F rollable resultLabel="Contact Type" captionPosition=top]{Magical Entity Contact}

A Magical Entity Campaign

A campaign driven by a magical entity patron might unfold according to this outline:

Levels 1–4. The campaign begins as the characters stumble into the entity’s domain and prove themselves against creatures the entity considers enemies. Aberrations such as @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmGrell000000000]{Grells}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmGrick000000000]{Gricks}, and @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmGrimlock000000]{Grimlocks} are all thematically appropriate foes.

Levels 5–10. The magical entity approaches the characters or invites them to the entity’s lair and offers to become their group patron, sending them on missions against monstrous foes. Githyanki and slaadi make good antagonists for this tier of play.

Levels 11–16. The mysterious mastermind controlling these Aberrations—whom the characters haven’t yet identified—captures or imprisons the magical entity, perhaps through the use of an Artifact, and the characters must rescue them. The characters battle @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmAboleth0000000]{Aboleths}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmBeholder000000]{Beholders}, @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmDeathTyrant000]{Death Tyrants}, and @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmMindFlayerArca]{Mind Flayer Arcanists}.

Levels 17–20. The mysterious mastermind is revealed as a creature similar to the group patron, but different in nature. For example, Bahamut is captured by a group of @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmAncientRedDrag]{Ancient Red Dragons}. Or Strahd is at the mercy of a powerful @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmLich0000000000]{Lich}, such as Acererak or Vecna. These two liches are further described in Vecna: Eve of Ruin, including game statistics for Vecna.

Political Faction.name: Political Faction
Political Faction.text:
A political faction group patron is tied to the governing structure of a magical realm. A political faction usually has great wealth and access to the realm’s resources, but the faction leaders are politicians and bureaucrats, not adventurers. Even if the leaders are powerful mages, they have no interest in risking their own lives. Instead, they hire the characters as spies or agents.

Campaigns with a political faction group patron combine high magic with political intrigue. The characters might be kept in the dark by their patron faction, which gives them only the information they absolutely need (and sometimes not even that). The faction sends the party into dangerous situations that force them to improvise.

Political Faction Motivations

A political faction might patronize a group for the following reasons:

The Characters Are Residents. If the characters live in the realm where the faction governs, the faction believes the characters are easier to recruit and more likely to be loyal. The faction might exert legal pressure on the characters, forcing them to do as the faction requires.

The Characters Are Foreign. The faction prefers to hire outsiders who can operate in neighboring realms without attracting attention, and who know the languages and customs of the faction’s rivals.

The Characters Are Deniable Assets. The political faction hires the adventures without official sanction. The party is sent on dangerous missions in far-off lands, and if they’re captured, the political faction denies any connection or responsibility for the party’s actions.

Political Faction Patrons

The following organizations, each detailed in Forgotten Realms: Heroes of Faerûn, could serve as political faction group patrons:

Red Wizards. The Red Wizards rule Thay, a land on the eastern edge of Faerûn in the Forgotten Realms. Thay is expansionist, and its rulers are mostly cruel tyrants. Thay and the Red Wizards are expanded on in Arcana Unleashed: Deadfall, which includes an adventure that embroils characters in a mission to kill Szass Tam, a Red Wizard lich who plots to once again control the nation.

Simbarch Council. Thay’s neighbor, the land of Aglarond, is ruled by a group of sorcerers called the Simbarch Council. In addition to governing the realm, the council trains sorcerers who come to Aglarond from across Faerûn. Aglarond has a long history of military conflict with Thay.

Witches of Rashemen. Rashemen is a land on Thay’s northern border. Rashemen is ruled by masked warlocks known as wychlaren, who make pacts with ancient spirits that dwell in Rashemen’s dense and magical forests. Like Aglarond, Rashemen has been invaded repeatedly by Thay, and some of the witches occasionally wish to strike at their longtime enemies.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.book.JournalEntry.aunArtHandoutsG2.JournalEntryPage.ickLgEORyUGAPsx0 classes=overlay-caption cite=false]

Creating Your Own Political Faction

Instead of using one of the political factions described above, you can create a political faction to serve as a group patron for your characters.

Political factions have a long history in the realms where they appear, and they’re distinguished by symbols, mottoes, and pass phrases. They require an oath, though some members of the faction are more loyal to that oath than others. Give some thought to the faction’s history and how its fortunes have risen or fallen over time. Give your faction at least one rival group in the same realm or a neighboring one; many adventures the characters undertake should be missions against a rival.

When you create a political faction for your campaign, you can roll on or choose from the Political Faction Type table to determine the faction’s nature.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.tables.RollTable.aunPoliticalFaDs rollable resultLabel="Patron Type" captionPosition=top]{Political Faction Type}

Political Faction Patron Perks

Characters in a party whose patron is a political faction gain the following perks.

Expenses and Salary. Your patron reimburses you for expenses incurred as part of your work. You are required to account for your expenses and must explain any extraordinary expenditures, but routine travel, ordinary equipment, and basic services don’t draw a second glance.

Additionally, your employment brings an income of 1 GP per day (enough to sustain a Modest lifestyle). At the DM’s discretion, your salary might increase or decrease depending on the faction’s nature, the type of work, and the length of your employment.

Immunity. As long as you remain in the political faction’s good graces, you can avoid prosecution for minor offenses under the laws of the realm where the faction is based. However, committing serious crimes, especially if they’re unrelated to assigned work, is a sure way to fall out of your patron’s good graces.

Powerful Allies. The political faction has secured alliances with powerful businesspeople, spellcasters, and tradespeople. The faction can call upon these allies to secure transportation for you by a means of your choosing (via coach, ship, or teleportation) at half the usual cost. When you take a Bastion turn, if you are level 9+, you can (as a group) issue the Recruit order to the political faction as if the faction was a Teleportation Circle facility in your Bastion. If you are level 17+, you can instead issue the Recruit order to the political faction as if it were a Guildhall facility within your Bastion.

Political Faction Contacts

A political faction has well-established procedures establishing how the characters communicate with their superiors, get to adventure sites, and return home when the mission is over. Procedures include rules for disguising communications, such as leaving messages in dead drops or protecting reports with the Illusory Script spell.

A political faction is large enough to include a cast of recurring characters, and the party might have a different contact for every mission. Alternatively, the party’s contact might change when a shift in government or evolving political philosophy forces the faction to adapt.

Roll on or choose from the Political Faction Contact table to determine who manages the relationship between the characters and the political faction.

@Embed[Compendium.dnd-arcana-unleashed.tables.RollTable.aunPoliticalFaaD rollable resultLabel="Contact Type" captionPosition=top]{Political Faction Contact}

A Political Faction Campaign

A campaign driven by a political faction patron might unfold according to this outline:

Levels 1–4. The characters are recruited by intermediaries and are unaware they’re serving the political faction. They receive a mission to infiltrate a rival faction and steal the spellbook of a well-protected @UUID[Compendium.dnd-monster-manual.actors.Actor.mmMage0000000000]{Mage}.

Levels 5–10. Having proven themselves, the characters are brought further into the faction and learn their employer’s identity. New missions send them to rival nations, where they sabotage rituals, steal magic items, plant incriminating evidence, and thwart plots to assassinate members of their patron faction.

Levels 11–16. The characters learn about a plot by a rival faction to assemble or retrieve an Artifact capable of great destruction in the realm where the patron faction is based. Retrieving and destroying the Artifact leads the characters on a grand adventure that visits multiple planes of existence.

Levels 17–20. A sudden and overwhelming strike by a rival faction eliminates most of the highest-ranking members of the patron faction, and the characters ascend into those positions. Now they must decide how to respond to the attack and settle the rivalry once and for all.

Trickster.name: Trickster
Trickster.text:
Tricksters are powerful beings—often archfey—who are known for their whimsical nature. A trickster can take many forms and might appear pleasant, angry, or simply otherworldly. But at their core, the trickster is unpredictable, their priorities and goals changing with the seasons or even from day to day.

Tricksters make good patrons for groups that prefer social interaction, exploration, and nonviolent conflict resolution over combat. Many tricksters prefer humiliating and pranking their enemies to killing them. Groups with a trickster patron are likely to spend time in the Feywild, visiting Domains of Delight and learning the distinctive rules of each.

Trickster Motivations

A trickster might patronize a group for the following reasons:

The Characters Are Interesting. Tricksters are like magpies, driven to collect shiny baubles. Adventurers are colorful, larger-than-life personalities who are likely to attract a trickster’s attention.

The Trickster Needs Plausible Deniability. A trickster makes enemies, and those enemies often instantly recognize the trickster and are alert to disguises. The trickster needs agents who aren’t known to be associated with the trickster.
